body.text:
I have a rather personal relationship with the web: somewhere between methodical curiosity and joyful entropy.

For me, a browsing session rarely follows a straight path. It starts with a question, veers off towards a tool, opens an article, three GitHub repositories and a video, then ends up with twelve thousand tabs spread across several windows, several browsers and sometimes several machines. This chaos isn’t just a bad habit: it’s also my way of exploring, connecting ideas and letting curiosity do its work.

The problem, of course, is finding what was really worth keeping.

A memory for my web

I’ve been compiling Digests for years. They’re a mix of monitoring logs, annotated bookmarks and snapshots of my current obsessions: artificial intelligence, developer tools, design, photography, publishing, digital fabrication, free software and curiosities that are hard to categorise.

This site transforms this accumulation into a more enduring archive. The links are deduplicated, stripped of their tracking parameters as far as possible, categorised by subject and accompanied by a short summary. The archives allow you to find every edition, and the tags highlight the themes that recur over time.

The selection remains deliberately personal. It is neither an exhaustive news feed nor an automated collection of everything that comes along. I keep what intrigues me, what might prove useful, what fuels an idea — and sometimes things I don’t yet know what to do with.

Why ‘Digest’?

The name is also a tribute to my grandad Richard. He was a subscriber to Reader’s Digest for almost his entire life. He used to make us read those books, talk to us about them and even give us the special children’s editions. Those volumes, which brought together stories, discoveries and windows onto the world, have always fascinated me.

Looking back, my Digest is, in a way, a continuation of that tradition: selecting, bringing together and passing on what has sparked curiosity. The medium has changed and the books have become links, but the desire remains the same — to share things that make you want to read, to understand and to explore further.

Images generated by code

Each edition automatically produces a unique poster measuring 1,200 × 627 pixels. It is not created by AI: it is entirely generated by a graphics generator developed for the Digest.

A SHA-256 hash of the date, title and description initialises a deterministic pseudo-random generator. The same edition therefore always retains the same image, whilst each new Digest is given its own composition.

The system chooses from three graphic families — collisions, screens or broken grids — and then varies the structure, colours, rotations, patterns, ink textures, noise and visual anomalies. The colour scheme combines red, black and paper with an accent colour. The description, date and number of links are automatically incorporated, with line breaks and text length managed accordingly.

The image is first constructed in SVG. It is then rendered using Resvg, utilising exclusively the Bricolage Grotesque font provided by the site, without relying on any fonts installed on the server. The resulting PNG is finally optimised using Sharp: the colour palette is limited to 256 colours, compression is set to maximum, and the file size is kept below 500 KB.

Chance plays a part in the composition, but never in the reproducibility of the result.

Share on LinkedIn

Sharing text, a URL and a large image simultaneously has proved unreliable with Open Graph previews and browser sharing tools.

The Digest therefore uses the LinkedIn API directly: the poster is uploaded as a media file, then linked to the text and URL of the edition. Before posting, a window allows you to draft the post, edit the hashtags generated from the Digest’s tags, and explicitly confirm publication.

This poster now has a square version measuring 1200 × 1200 pixels, distinct from the rectangular Open Graph image. It spans the full width of the feed. In the full-screen desktop viewer, LinkedIn may add two dark grey bands to centre the square within a taller column: these are part of the LinkedIn interface, not the image itself.

Uploading is synchronous, so that the post is only created once the image has actually been processed. A resource that has already been published remains reusable: the ‘Repost on LinkedIn’ action reopens the composer, allows you to change the text and hashtags, and then creates a new post without deleting the previous ones. The Digest thus retains a history of repeat posts whilst preventing concurrent submissions and unintended duplicates.

Geek, printer and photographer

I’m Marc Tallec, a geek for long enough to have experienced several iterations of the Web, but also a printer and photographer. I enjoy understanding how a tool works just as much as seeing what it can be used to create: an image, a book, an interface, a service or a new way of working.

You can find my personal work at marctallec.com. Together with Claire, I’m also developing OOBLIK, our studio dedicated to imagery, print and editorial objects.

This Digest is therefore my space for reflection: an attempt to transform the noise, the open windows and my digital entropy into something shareable — the bits worth keeping… or not.

A single agent is merely a proof of concept. As soon as there are twenty of them working together, roles must be allocated, data must be retained, code must be isolated, budgets must be monitored and a decision must be made as to who can shut down the system. This edition maps out twenty open-source projects that transform agents into teams, swarms or enterprises: from the most mature orchestration engines to the new ‘agent-based OSes’.

The term ‘OS’ is used here as a metaphor. These projects do not replace Linux, macOS or Windows: they add a control layer responsible for assigning work, maintaining state, managing tools and supervising agents that can continue to operate once the conversation has ended. Their maturity is therefore measured not only by the number of GitHub stars, but also by fault tolerance, observability, safeguards and execution isolation.

My top editorial picks

To create a coherent collection rather than a simple directory, seven key themes emerge:

  1. Paperclip, for the explicit transformation of agents into an organisation. Organisational charts, objectives, budgets and approvals turn the metaphor of the artificial company into a genuine management tool.
  2. CrewAI, for the metaphor of specialised teams that has now become mainstream. Agents are assigned a role, an objective and complementary tasks within the same crew.
  3. LangGraph, for explaining the deterministic engine behind sustainable systems. Its state graphs make branching paths, resumptions and human interventions visible.
  4. Microsoft Agent Framework, as a sign of industry standardisation. The successor to AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, it combines multi-agent orchestration, persistent state and interoperability in Python and .NET.
  5. MetaGPT and ChatDev, for the history of the simulated software company. Product, architecture, development and quality control become functions distributed amongst agents.
  6. OpenClaw and Hermes Agent, as a new generation of persistent ‘employees’. They reside in messaging systems and terminals, remembering, automating and delegating tasks to their own sub-agents.
  7. E2B, to remind us that an agent farm also requires isolation and infrastructure. Without sandboxing, resource control and the separation of secrets, autonomy remains, above all, an operational risk.

Three layers rather than a single OS

Frameworks such as LangGraph, Google ADK, OpenAI Agents SDK and Microsoft Agent Framework form the engine: they describe transitions, handoffs and execution rules. Paperclip, CrewAI, MetaGPT and ChatDev add the social dimension: teams, hierarchies, responsibilities and shared objectives. Finally, E2B, Daytona and OpenHands’ controlled environments provide the technical foundation upon which agents can actually operate.

Between these layers lie Letta’s memory, the observability provided by AgentScope or the NeMo Agent Toolkit, and evaluation harnesses such as AWorld. It is their combination—rather than any single project in isolation—that is beginning to resemble an operating system for agent collectives.

The full report

The twenty fact sheets below allow for a comparison of these approaches, ranging from the most widely deployed components to proposals that are still at the experimental stage.

body.text:
The traditional IDE organises files, an editor, a terminal and a debugger. The ADE now organises agents. This shift in terminology signals a more profound transformation: the unit of work is no longer simply the file opened by a developer, but the task entrusted to an agent in an isolated environment.

The central argument of this edition can be summed up in a single sentence: the next essential tool for AI developers may be neither the model nor the editor. It will be the orchestrator.

From the IDE to the ADE

For thirty years, the integrated development environment (IDE) has brought together in a single window everything a human needs to programme: file tree, editor, terminal, debugger, search and version control. Code assistants first found their place within this architecture in the form of smarter autocomplete or a conversation panel.

Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other terminal agents are now shifting the centre of gravity. They read the repository, modify multiple files, run tests, inspect errors and sometimes even prepare the commit or pull request themselves. Humans no longer handle every line of code: they assign tasks, monitor execution and assess the results.

The dominant workflow therefore takes on a different form:

Project → tasks → Git worktrees → independent agents → supervision → diff and review → merge

The IDE — Agentic Development Environment — becomes less of an editor and more of a control centre. Its role is to launch multiple agents, provide them with the correct context, isolate their changes, flag those awaiting a decision and present their proposals in a comparable manner.

The worktree as a common primitive

Most of these tools converge on the same building block: the Git worktree. A task is assigned a separate branch and a separate working directory. Claude Code can fix a regression whilst Codex prepares a feature and OpenCode explores a third solution, without their changes immediately mixing.

This isolation does not solve everything. Contributors may still modify the same concepts on different branches, fail to set up the project, or produce incompatible changes at the time of merging. But the worktree transforms a cacophony of concurrent processes into observable, comparable and, if necessary, disposable units.

It becomes to the ADE what the file was to the IDE: the concrete object around which the interface organises the work.

The stable layer above the models

Models will remain uneven. Claude will excel at one task, Codex at another, and Gemini or a local model at a third. Their performance, pricing and context windows will evolve rapidly. Betting the entire workflow on just one of them is tantamount to confusing the engine of the moment with the vehicle.

The ADE offers a more stable layer: project + context + worktrees + agents + supervision + validation + history. The model becomes an interchangeable executor that one chooses according to the problem, cost or confidentiality constraints.

This promise remains partly to be proven. Not all agents expose the same events, session formats or recovery mechanisms. Changing models does not yet mean cleanly transferring their memory and reasoning. But the direction is clear: the environment seeks to absorb these differences to offer the developer a consistent workflow.

Frame 326 stars Apache 2.0 Specifications and background
ADE 94 stars AGPL 3.0 Desktop, CLI and mobile

These figures were taken from the official repositories on 28 August 2026. They give an indication of the rate of adoption, not of absolute quality. A small community can support a more robust architecture than a high-profile project, whilst a large number of stars guarantees neither stability nor longevity.

Three projects that define the category

Orca — the most comprehensive cockpit

Orca embodies the concept of a fleet most directly. It runs CLI agents side by side, each in its own worktree, then brings together terminals, files, diffs, GitHub, Linear, remote machines and notifications into a single interface. Its mobile companion also allows you to monitor or restart a run whilst away from your workstation.

Its most revealing feature is the ability to send the same problem to several isolated agents and then compare their solutions. Development becomes almost like concurrent experimentation: multiple implementations are produced, tested and compared before a human chooses or merges them.

Licensed under the MIT licence and driven by a very strong community, Orca is currently the best starting point for understanding what a general-purpose IDE could become.

Emdash — the vendor-agnostic open-source choice

Emdash explicitly defines itself as an open-source agent-based development environment. Its Apache 2.0 licence and vendor independence make it the clearest candidate for building a sustainable workflow without tying it to a single agent.

Its approach follows the actual development pipeline: a ticket from GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira or Asana is assigned to an agent in an isolated environment; this is followed by changes, review, testing, the pull request and CI. Agents can also work on a remote machine via SSH whilst the interface remains local.

Emdash is less spectacular than Orca, but its neutrality and integration with project tools probably make it the most coherent open-source choice in this selection.

Superset — the integrated agent-based IDE

Superset uses the same basic building blocks — a task, an isolated workspace, an agent — with an ambition closer to that of a direct successor to the IDE. It maintains sessions via a daemon, flags agents requiring attention, displays diffs and allows workspaces to be opened in other editors.

The project claims to be able to orchestrate over a hundred agents. This figure primarily describes an architectural capacity: no human can reasonably examine a hundred complex workflows at once. It nevertheless raises the right question: that of attention. When ten agents are running simultaneously, the problem is no longer launching them but knowing which one is blocked, which one has finished and which one requires a decision.

An editorial distinction is essential: Superset releases its code under the Elastic Licence 2.0. It can be used, modified and self-hosted, but this licence is not recognised as open source in the strict sense by the OSI. Superset is therefore source-available, not strictly open source.

The alternative approach: staying in the terminal

Agent Deck rejects the idea that an agent dashboard must necessarily become a large graphical application. Written in Go and built around tmux, it brings together sessions, their statuses, notifications, groups and worktrees within a terminal interface.

This approach tackles the same problem using existing Unix primitives. It will appeal more to developers who already work in tmux and want to monitor multiple agents without installing a new Electron-based IDE. Above all, Agent Deck demonstrates that an IDE is a function first and a graphical interface second.

Two up-and-coming projects to watch

OpenADE, licensed under the MIT licence, advocates a more structured workflow: plan, review, then execute. Plans can be compared across multiple agents before a single agent applies the changes. The environment remains local and brings together the terminal, files, search, diff, process management and Git snapshots centred around Claude Code and Codex.

ADE literally takes its name from the category. Still in its infancy, this AGPL project comprises a macOS application, a CLI, a persistent local runtime — the ‘brain’ — and an iOS companion. Each task resides in its own worktree, and the various interfaces connect to the same execution state. Its adoption remains limited, but its architecture clearly illustrates the idea of a sustainable environment to which multiple interfaces are attached.

After orchestration, the project’s memory

Frame shifts the focus to a problem that cockpits do not yet solve effectively: how do we preserve the software’s intent? Running five agents in parallel is pointless if each one has to rediscover the architecture, past decisions and acceptance criteria.

Its spec-driven approach transforms planning, architecture notes, structure and tasks into a persistent context, readable by future agents and versioned alongside the project. Frame is less a fleet manager than an attempt to build the collective memory that this fleet will require.

This approach could become just as important as orchestration itself. A mature ADE will need to answer not only ‘which agent is working on which branch?’, but also ‘what do they know about the project, why was this decision made, and how can they prove that their work adheres to the original intention?’

Agent, ADE, organisation: three distinct layers

Confusion with ‘agent-based operating systems’ disappears if we separate the layers:

Agent — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI: to execute a development task.

IDE — Orca, Emdash, Superset: isolating, launching, supervising, comparing and validating multiple agents.

Organisational orchestration — Paperclip and multi-agent systems: distributing objectives, responsibilities, budgets and governance across an organisation.

Paperclip aims to become the operating system for an enterprise of agents. Orca and Emdash aim to become the operating system for its software workshop. They are closely related, sometimes required to connect, but they do not solve the same problem.

My editorial ranking

Orca is currently the most comprehensive suite and the project that best defines the category. Emdash is the cleanest open-source choice for a workflow-agnostic solution. Superset perhaps embodies the product vision closest to the future IDE, with the significant caveat of its source-available licence.

Next come Agent Deck for terminal-based development, OpenADE for planning, Frame for memory and context, and then ADE for its local, persistent and mobile architecture – which is still at an experimental stage.

The real test, however, will not be the number of agents displayed in an interface. It will be the ability to make them replaceable, to resume their work after a failure, to preserve the project’s intent, and to narrow down a hundred competing proposals to a verifiable human decision.

The IDE helped the developer to write code. The ADE must now help them to manage those who write it.

These rules describe the data processed by the OOBLIK Digest — Curation Chrome and Firefox extension, how it is used, and the choices available to the user.

The sole purpose of the extension is to manually save the active page to OOBLIK Digest’s private editorial queue in preparation for a future issue. It is intended for the owner of the Digest.

Data processed

The extension only reads a page following an explicit action on its icon or via its keyboard shortcut. It may then pre-populate the form with:

  • the address of the active page and its canonical address, if any;
  • its title and meta description;
  • any text selected by the user;
  • the category, summary and tags entered or corrected in the form;
  • a private editorial note entered by the user.

This data relates primarily to browsing history and the content of the website, as defined in the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons policies. The extension does not monitor browsing, does not maintain any general history and does not collect any data in the background.

Time of transmission and purpose

All information is displayed in the form before it is submitted. It is only transmitted when the ‘Save draft’ button is clicked, via HTTPS, to digest.ooblik.com.

It is used exclusively to:

  • pre-filling and saving a private editorial draft;
  • detect duplicates;
  • prepare, proofread and voluntarily publish an edition of the Digest;
  • ensuring the technical and editorial traceability of publications.

The extension does not use the data for advertising, profiling, commercial audience measurement, credit checks or any other purpose.

Private data and publication

The selected text and editorial note remain private. They are never added to the public catalogue, the public archives or Git commits.

The URL, title, summary, category and tags only become public after publication has been explicitly confirmed via the admin panel. This publication is a separate action from saving the draft.

Storage and deletion

Drafts are stored in the administration service’s private database. An active draft can be edited or deleted via the administration panel.

After publication, its private revision history may be retained to ensure traceability, idempotent recovery and deduplication. Private notes remain private during this retention period. Metadata that has been deliberately published follows the Digest’s editorial retention policy.

Authentication, access and sharing

The service requires the authorised owner’s GitHub session. No GitHub tokens or administration secrets are read or stored by the extension.

Data is neither sold, nor used for advertising, nor passed on to third parties for their own use. GitHub receives only the metadata that the owner explicitly chooses to publish, for the purposes of versioning and deploying the Digest.

Security

Communications between the extension and digest.ooblik.com use HTTPS. The administration service requires owner authentication, restricts authorised origins and stores its data on a private server.

The extension does not use any remote code: all JavaScript executed is included in the packages distributed via the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons.

Browser permissions

  • activeTab allows the URL and title of the active tab to be read only following a user action;
  • scripting allows the canonical URL, meta description and selected text to be extracted on an ad hoc basis;
  • access to https://digest.ooblik.com/* allows the session to be verified and the draft to be saved in the private admin panel.

The extension does not request access to all websites, nor does it request access to the cookies API.

Firefox also displays, prior to installation, the categories of data required: browsingActivity and websiteContent. These correspond solely to the URL and content that the user chooses to save manually.

Limited use

The use of information received by the extension complies with the Chrome Web Store and Firefox Add-ons regulations regarding user data, including Chrome’s ‘Limited Use’ requirements. The data is used solely to provide the curation feature described on this page.

Changes and contact

Any substantial changes to these practices will be published on this page and notified within the extension where required.

If you have any questions, please use the contact details provided on the About page.

Requests and exchanges

The project therefore does not begin with a bookmarking service. It builds on hand-written Digests, fed by the OOBLIK blogs and by posts shared over the years on Tumblr, Instagram and other social media platforms. The changes reflect four successive requirements:

  1. to make the old HTML Digests searchable again.
  2. to bring together links from WordPress blogs and social media feeds without erasing their sources.
  3. to have a static, readable Digest, organised and deployable without revealing any server secrets to GitHub.
  4. to make this diverse archive searchable by archives and tags.

The restoration revealed two editorial considerations: missing resources deserve to be preserved and documented, whilst old, empty Mailchimp editions provide no useful historical record.

Decisions

  • Hugo and PaperMod form the public backbone.
  • data/links.json centralises the links. The archives consist of dated Hugo content.
  • The Digest is not a platform migration: it brings together multiple sources, multiple websites and multiple generations of URLs.
  • GitHub Actions creates a ‘production’ branch. CloudPanel takes over without any webhooks or server credentials in GitHub.
  • A dead public URL remains viewable and is flagged as such.
  • Domain variants and the actual validity of the destination must be verified, not just their HTTP response.
  • All external links open in a new tab.

Implementation

The first commit adds the theme, the homepage, the archives, the tags, the catalogue and the curation skill. The validation and deployment workflows follow immediately.

The first historical restoration brings back old editions and several social feeds. A Pinboard export is one of the technical sources processed that day, alongside other batches: it is neither the core of the Digest nor its origin. The import tools, consistency checks and the concept of ‘lien-mort’ instead provide a common method for these fragments. Imported titles are cleaned up, external links corrected and the tag explorer is given a dedicated interface.

Above all, this first day marks the start of a wider project. Posts from WordPress blogs, notably the OOBLIK Blog, will subsequently be added to the same repository along with their text and provenance. Tumblr, Instagram and other feeds will retain their identity rather than being merged into a single source.

Mailchimp entries that no longer contained a usable destination and six entirely empty editions have been removed. This deletion concerns import artefacts, not documented defunct public resources.

Validation and deployment

The added workflows validate the data and then build Hugo. The 16 GitHub Actions runs visible for the day were successful, with no failures. The final deployment goes through the `production` branch and is handled by CloudPanel.

Requests and discussions

The following decisions were explicitly clarified during the conversation:

  • launch via the Chrome icon and a configurable shortcut.
  • A compact, pre-filled form and quick registration.
  • A private queue allowing users to select 10, 20 links or more.
  • Publication of a single Digest for the selected batch.
  • Use restricted to the owner only.
  • Title, category, summary and at least one tag are required for publication.
  • Suggested date and title; editable introduction and SEO description.
  • Categories and titles sorted alphabetically.
  • Blocked if the date already has a Digest.
  • Digest metadata can be edited after publication.
  • Tracking through to GitHub Actions validation and deployment to production.
  • Unlisted release on the Chrome Web Store with automatic updates.

Preparation for the Web Store then focused on the extension’s stable ID, the package, the icon, the screenshots, the description, the permission justifications and the privacy policy. The submission moved to ‘pending review’ status.

Decisions

  • Hugo remains the public site. admin-service is the sole backend.
  • The extension never communicates directly with GitHub.
  • Incomplete drafts are permitted, but their publication is blocked.
  • The taxonomy comes exclusively from the existing catalogue.
  • Private, local, authenticated or sensitive URLs are not permitted.
  • An active duplicate reopens the draft. A published link redirects to its administration page.
  • The catalogue and archive are written in a single commit.
  • Publication is idempotent and retries once following a GitHub conflict.
  • Private notes and selections never leave the private area.
  • The server only accepts the exact origin of the Web Store extension.
  • The extension uses Manifest V3, WXT and TypeScript without React.

Implementation

Viewing and history

Week 15 of 2017 has been added. The home page now features filters by date, random selection and favourites. Navigation and the archives have been improved. Broken links can point to a Wayback Machine archive whilst retaining their original URL.

Administration

The proprietary service adds Better Auth, the GitHub App, visibility modification and the /admin interface. Public deletion is deliberately discreet and separate from ordinary actions. A port conflict is resolved prior to deployment.

Curation and publication

SQLite stores drafts and publications. The APIs cover taxonomy options, CRUD, preview, publication, links and edits.

Publishing revalidates all data on the server side, enforces unique dates, creates stable UUIDs, writes two files per commit and follows SHA-related workflows. Shared fixtures align TypeScript and Python normalisation.

Extension and Chrome Web Store

The extension captures the URL, title, canonical, meta description and selection following an explicit action. Permissions are limited to activeTab, scripting and https://digest.ooblik.com/*.

The Web Store ID used is nlejcccmpbajpoaknlecegkpgdegiflf. Icons and promotional visuals are generated and stored at browser-extension/store-assets/. The public page /confidentialite/ describes the voluntary collection of data, its limited use and the permissions required. A link to this page is placed in the footer after ‘Admin’.

Operation

Two successive patches have improved the PM2 restart process when changing releases or when a previously stopped process needs to be recreated.

Validation and deployment

Prior to submission, the tests and type checks for the administration and the extension are passed, as are the catalogue checks and the Hugo build. The catalogue now contains 3,979 consistent links and 835 editions.

The workflows Validate and Deploy production are followed for changes to the extension, privacy policy and footer. The public result is checked after the CloudPanel handover.

body.text:
The eclipse as a method

On 12 August, the sun disappears just enough to remind us that one form can become more legible when another recedes. This is a good definition of the design of the Digest: not adding decoration, but organising the absences, the intervals, the black spaces and what must remain visible.

The journal therefore does not seek to resemble a blog. It borrows from Swiss design its explicit grid, its firm alignments and its unambiguous hierarchy. It borrows from the architect’s title block the adjoining cells, the shared lines, the date, the folio number and the sense that a page belongs to a larger whole. The result builds on the language developed in *From the Swiss Cartouche to the Memory of the OOBLIK Blog*, but applies it here to the construction phase rather than to categories.

Black provides the structure. Off-white retains the warmth of the paper. Grey carries the metadata without obscuring it. Coral serves as a signal: a number, an active marker, a hover link, a small burst of light in an almost monochrome composition. As during an eclipse, the colour derives its power solely from its scarcity.

Two typographic voices

Bricolage Grotesque carries the headings. Its width, its irregularities and its energy prevent the grid from becoming bureaucratic. It can be monumental in a post, dense on a map, and retain a very physical presence when the heading spans several lines.

JetBrains Mono handles everything else: dates, summaries, captions, links, technical snippets. This monospace typeface bears the mark of the tool and the source file. It conveys that the journal is not only written, but also constructed. The duo avoids two pitfalls: a Swiss modernity that is too museum-like and a development interface that is too literal.

American posters from the 1940s and 1950s add a third voice. They do not serve as nostalgic wallpaper: their solid colours, diagonals and graphic effectiveness respond to the grid. In the index, they form cropped banners. In the article, they revert to square objects, attributed to and linked with their public collection.

To explore in the Digest: design, typography and graphic design.

Building in dialogue with Codex

The page did not emerge from a perfect specification. It took shape as we watched it come to life. I describe an intention — ‘architect’s cartouche’, ‘more dense’, ‘the title must breathe’, ‘no bullet points’ — and Codex translates this direction into Hugo templates, CSS, responsive rules and tests.

This division of labour is important. I retain control over the direction, the aesthetic, the memory of the project and the right to say when something feels off. I leave the technical side to Codex: finding the right file, understanding the content adapter, preserving the nine existing posts, setting up the RSS feed, checking the previous and next links, preventing mobile overflow, and then displaying the result in a real browser.

The prompt isn’t a magic command. It’s a design tool. An initial formulation provides a structure. A screenshot allows us to highlight a detail. Hovering reveals a colour that’s too muted. The mobile view shows excessive density. We make corrections, reload, compare. Testing then takes over to transform a visual preference into a lasting rule.

This approach ties in with Administration and curation via Chrome: the tool is not separate from its use. The browser is for viewing, Codex for building and verifying, and Git for keeping a record. The technology becomes accessible without taking centre stage.

A journal made up of links

The Digest was born out of a somewhat unreasonable passion for URLs. An address is tiny, but it holds a promise: someone has published something somewhere, and accepts that we can access it without asking permission from a platform.

Collecting a link isn’t just about setting it aside. It’s about giving it a fitting title, a few words of context, tags, a date and a place amongst other discoveries. It’s about creating a way back for yourself, and then a way in for others. Archives, the Internet, the Web’s memory and the Web itself are not static shelves: they enable connections that search engines and algorithmic feeds no longer offer.

Internal links matter just as much as external ones. They connect the different stages of the project: the creation of the Digest and the restoration of lost links, the revival of tags, and finally the legacy of the OOBLIK Blog. The journal thus forms neither a closed chronology nor a cold record, but a map in which each post can reopen several paths.

Learning to love 404s

A 404 error does not erase what once existed. It merely changes its status. Where an ordinary catalogue would delete an address that has become obsolete, the Digest retains it, marks it as dead and documents what it once allowed us to see. Absence becomes information.

This attention is not a cult of ruins. It champions a simple idea of the open internet: pages published at their own addresses, freely linked, copied, cited and shared without restriction. Domains change hands, services close down, names move on. Preserving the original URL ensures that history is not rewritten after the event.

The launch of the Digest already established this principle by bringing together scattered HTML Digests, blogs and social feeds. The journal now gives it a visible form. The nets are the connections, the cells are the fragments of memory, and the coral marks what remains active amidst the disappearances.

Long-term decisions

  • keep ‘Bricolage Grotesque’ for titles and ‘JetBrains Mono’ for the text.
  • Use the coral as a subtle highlight, particularly when hovering over headings.
  • Design the navigation like an architect’s title block, never as a collection of rounded buttons.
  • Build with Codex through visible iterations, then convert the choices into reproducible tests.
  • Increase the number of internal links between posts, tags and archives.
  • Keep dead URLs for reference without hiding their status.
  • Reserve LinkedIn posting for explicit action by the administration.

Note on provenance

This post is a retrospective design note, based on the visual and editorial choices made during the project. It does not claim to reproduce word for word a recorded conversation, nor to attribute to 12 August any commits made after that date.

Continuation

Continue to write the journal as one might tend a constellation: adding points, linking days, noting extinctions and leaving enough space for a new path to emerge.

Requests and correspondence

The requests recorded in the plans and documentation concerned:

  • simplifying the publication process and providing immediate feedback on its actual progress.
  • automatic resumption of tracking after an interruption.
  • a more visible OOBLIK identity in the browser and in social media previews.
  • a large LinkedIn image, followed by a native post where the text remains editable.
  • a customised configuration of LinkedIn credentials without exposing secrets to the browser.
  • The option to share either an entire edition or a specific link.
  • Correction of editorial destinations without losing their history.

The remainder of this summary is reconstructed from the commits and their diffs. The full conversations are not stored in the repository.

Decisions

  • Progress tracking uses four server states — preparation, validation, deployment and release — and no fake percentages.
  • A single timer tracks the publication process and resumes after a page refresh, a return to the tab or a temporary network error.
  • The production workflow builds Hugo once and deploys that same output.
  • The site version is visible in the footer and follows SemVer.
  • Social media images are deterministic, versioned and limited to an optimised 1200 × 627 PNG.
  • Native LinkedIn sharing is an admin action. Secrets and tokens are encrypted in SQLite and are never sent back to the browser.
  • The suggested text, including hashtags, remains editable before submission.
  • Correcting or reactivating a link preserves its identity and editorial history.

Development

Publication and operation

The redundant preview button has been removed in favour of a single action. A four-segment progress bar displays the persistent states, resumes automatically and leads to public publication. Line breaks are standardised to ensure consistency when switching between Windows and WSL.

The Hugo build avoids repeated searches in the catalogue. Production validates the sources and the extension, builds once, then publishes this artefact to the production branch. The extension’s archive is also verified in CI. The footer now displays the site version.

Brand identity and social media images

OOBLIK favicons are added for the site, Safari, iOS and the admin panel. A deterministic graphic system generates a social poster for each archive, with a grid, typography, flat colours and variants derived from the content. The images are included in the social metadata and visible on the editing pages. Long lists of posters are paginated.

Catalogue editing

A link’s URL can now be edited via the admin panel. Several corrected destinations, including Éditions GwinZegal, are reactivated following verification of their identity. A YouTube entry is corrected without deleting its history.

LinkedIn publication

The author now has access to an enlarged, refreshable preview, and can then post a large image accompanied by text and a link. The mechanism is now a native integration with the LinkedIn API via OAuth, configurable via /admin, with encryption of credentials and the token, customisable text and automatic addition of hashtags. The action remains invisible outside the admin panel and now finally supports the sharing of an individual link.

The ‘About’ page also documents the technical and editorial background to the Digest.

Validation and deployment

  • Initial testing of the publication tracking feature comprised 39 successful admin tests and 70 successful extension tests, using TypeScript compilation and a Hugo build.
  • Subsequent developments added contract tests for social media images, LinkedIn configuration, OAuth, native publishing and administration actions.
  • The majority of the work was merged into main via pull requests nos. 17 to 43. The detailed status of the workflows can still be viewed in GitHub Actions.

title.text: Publication, visual identity and sharing on LinkedIn

body.text:
Requests and discussions

This summary has been compiled from the commits and their tests:

  • align the owner actions with the relevant links.
  • correct the display of bookmarks when the list is filtered.
  • No longer rely on a remote favicon that is missing or cached.
  • Ensure that when a link is shared, the image is genuinely specific to its destination.
  • Retain a usable image when the remote screenshot fails.
  • Audit and then harden the automated browser’s network perimeter.
  • Preserve the end of long LinkedIn texts and release all interrupted connections.

Decisions

  • Administrative actions remain server-side and restricted to the owning session, even when they appear in public lists.
  • A missing favicon uses an explicit local asset. Domain exceptions are versioned data and their cache is invalidated along with the other assets.
  • A link image prioritises a screenshot of the first screen, converted to black and white and overlaid with the title, domain and coral ink.
  • A site failure produces a typographic map specific to the link, never the generic banner for that edition.
  • Application-level URL validation is coupled with a pinned DNS resolution at the Chromium transport layer.
  • Streams, persistent media and connections not required for a static capture are blocked. Pending tunnels are limited and terminated along with their client.
  • When a LinkedIn text needs to be shortened, its conclusion and link are preserved.

Implementation

Administration and viewing

Link details display the options to edit, view and share when the owner is logged in. List filtering ensures no favourite remains in an inconsistent visual state. A demonstration resource is hidden in accordance with the editorial retention policy.

Resilient favicons

A local fallback replaces unavailable icons. A table of known domains allows this fallback to be selected directly, and the asset’s URL follows the site’s versioning to prevent an old response from remaining in the cache.

Link-specific images

The service opens the destination’s first screen in Chromium, disables animations, crops the image to 1200 × 627, converts it to black and white, then adds an OOBLIK banner. The result is named based on the link’s identifier and content, written atomically and stored in the shared directory. An action allows you to force its regeneration.

If navigation fails, a deterministic typographic SVG is rendered as a PNG containing the resource’s title and domain.

Network boundary and LinkedIn robustness

The main destination and each sub-resource are checked. A local proxy resolves each public host once, caches its address and connects Chromium directly to that address. Local networks, private addresses, unexpected protocols, non-standard ports and persistent resources are rejected.

The latest patches limit the buffer of a pending HTTPS tunnel, close the upstream connection as soon as the browser disconnects, and prevent a long LinkedIn text from losing its conclusion during normalisation.

Windows environment

Following the discontinuation of WSL for local development, the two directories ` node_modules` have been recreated on Windows to replace the native Linux binaries for Sharp, Rollup and other build tools. The README now specifies that switching between Windows, WSL and Linux requires this reinstallation and that node_modules must never be shared.

The extension audit also updates two transitive development dependencies, brace-expansion and nanoid, without changing the direct dependencies or the extension’s behaviour.

Validation and deployment

  • The changes are accompanied by tests covering admin actions, favicons, fallback rendering, Chromium capture, DNS pinning, buffer limits and socket closure.

title.text: Stricter editorial measures and LinkedIn screenshots

body.text:
Requests and discussions

  • Replace the rectangular LinkedIn poster with a true square that takes up more space in the feed.
  • Maintain the same behaviour for administration and for directly sharing a link.
  • Regenerate the square versions of all past posts.
  • Understand why a post accepted by the API results in ‘This post cannot be displayed’.
  • Allow a retry without silently creating a duplicate.
  • Close the modal at the right time and remove a second confirmation that has become superfluous.
  • Check whether the dark grey bands visible in the viewer are part of the image.

The final successful attempt results in a visible post with its square image. It confirms both the technical correction and the design choice.

Decisions

  • The Open Graph image remains at 1200 × 627. LinkedIn receives a dedicated file of 1200 × 1200.
  • Historical posts retain both formats. Future generations and backfills must maintain this pair going forward.
  • Screenshots specific to links are also composed as a square.
  • The dark grey bands at the top and bottom of the large LinkedIn viewer are accepted: they result from its container being taller than it is wide and must not be included or compensated for in the PNG.
  • The legacy Assets API is used in ‘SYNCHRONOUS_UPLOAD’ mode so that the creation of the post waits for the image to be processed.
  • A URL remains protected against duplicates. Republishing is only permitted via the explicit action ‘Repost if the post is inaccessible’.
  • This button already conveys a sufficiently clear intention. An additional confirmation box complicates the user journey without making it any more secure.

Implementation

Two formats for each edition

The generator produces a 1200 × 627 Open Graph poster and a 1200 × 1200 LinkedIn variant from the same deterministic identity. The 836 historical editions have been completed, and the backfill tools now maintain both outputs. The publication validator accepts the paths for these square variants.

Square for direct sharing

The screenshot of a link’s first screen is redrawn within a square canvas. The composer detects the PNG’s natural dimensions and displays the preview without imposing the old aspect ratio. The typographical fallback follows the same format.

From false success to synchronous upload

An initial attempt returns a LinkedIn URN and a ‘creation successful’ status, but the post is missing from the profile and its URL remains inaccessible. The cause is a race condition between the asynchronous processing of the asset and the creation of the post. The save operation now requires SYNCHRONOUS_UPLOAD. The request to publish is only sent once the upload has completed.

Retrieval without hidden duplicates

The URN from the false success had been cached, so a new attempt on the same URL would normally return ‘already published’. The interface then offers the option to republish, which removes this single association, re-establishes an atomic lock and executes the corrected workflow.

For an archive, the modal closes to reveal the result and its button on the page. When the message exists only within the modal, the modal remains open. The additional native confirmation has ultimately been removed.

Validation and deployment

  • The suite now has 114 successful tests, with checks dedicated to square images, synchronous uploads, deduplication, retries and the behaviour of modal windows.
  • The TypeScript build succeeds after each fix.
  • Pull requests 64 to 76 pass GitHub Actions validation. The main LinkedIn changes are delivered via PRs 70 to 76.
  • The public and admin versions are verified after deployment, up to v1.8.6, then the corresponding annotated Git tags are pushed.
  • The final test on LinkedIn produces a visible, properly formatted post that is correctly linked to its text and URL.

title.text: The LinkedIn feed: from false success to a visible post

body.text:
Requests and discussions

The day began with a simple need: to be able to manage the main categories without having to edit the files manually. The discussion then broadened the scope to their editorial significance, with the search for a name capable of encompassing philosophy, sociology, ideological struggles and climate, then moved on to defining Krisis and adding a description for each category.

The existing public display, consisting of rounded icons, seemed too generic and difficult to scale up. The preference expressed for Swiss precision and architectural cartouches set the direction for the new design scheme.

Decisions taken

  • The taxonomy is managed from a dedicated section within the administration.
  • A category has a name and a description, even before it contains a link.
  • The public site displays all configured categories, including those with zero entries.
  • Navigation uses a grid of numbered rectangular title blocks.
  • Selecting a box highlights it on the left and reveals the description on the right. The layout switches to a vertical layout on mobile devices.
  • The animations remain informative, accessible and optional.

Changes made

  • adding, renaming and deleting categories via the admin panel.
  • Safe migration of links when renaming, and prevention of the deletion of a category that is still in use.
  • Addition and editing of the ‘description’ field.
  • Categories ‘Cultures & Combats’ and ‘Photographie’ added to the catalogue.
  • Replacement of ‘pills’ with a typographic register featuring lines.
  • Focus mode with descriptive card, explicit back button and keyboard control.
  • Précédent · Folio · Suivant pagination standardised into a compact cartouche without rounded corners.
  • Pagination reset to the actual start of the grid, just below the sticky block, after each folio change.
  • Category counters calculated across all their public links, whilst keeping feeds outside the general Tout filter.
  • Display of empty categories and a fallback message when the description is missing.
  • Successive versions: v1.9.0, v1.10.0 and then v1.11.0.

Importing archives from the OOBLIK blog

Version v1.12.0 adds a one-off, reversible import from a WordPress WXR export. The default mode only generates a validation report. Missing, duplicate, private or redirected posts are never published automatically. The selected posts are added to the feed blog-ooblik and the ‘OOBLIK Blog Archives’ category, and therefore remain outside Tout. Their local images are standardised as 16:9 WebP banners without rounded corners, also available in the modal window.

The patch v1.12.1 enables a subsequent run to recognise these same maps by their destination and source, so as to add the FTP images without recreating the links or altering their IDs.

The patch v1.12.2 reintegrates the 280 WXR posts into Tout, without restoring the old social feeds, and explicitly converts the WordPress categories Photo, Photographes, Argentique, Camera Porn and Exposition into the ‘Digest’ category Photographie, then Livre / Book into Design & Création. The photograph takes precedence when a post also belongs to the ‘book’ category. The other WordPress taxonomies remain as tags, and posts with no matching category retain the archive category.

The visual fix v1.12.3 tightens the internal margins of the category boxes and prevents words from being split in the middle. Développement and Photographie thus remain intact, whilst compound titles can still wrap to the next line between two words. The calendar adopts the same geometry without rounded corners: the panel, navigation, days and markers are square. The current date is filled with the accent colour and the selected date has a square outline.

The ‘v1.13.0’ feature adds a second round of data retrieval for the 525 posts without a ‘Source’ block. The analysis identifies 290 unique external destinations and 63 ambiguous groups. 171 posts with no leads whatsoever are compiled into a standalone HTML review page. The example WordPress post is excluded. The choices are stored locally and can be exported as a overrides.json, without implicit publication.

The following editorial decision treats the 171 posts without a destination as standalone publications, rather than as errors. The import now retains the full text, cleaned of all WordPress posts, including the 280 already present, whilst keeping a short summary on the map. The full text can be viewed in the modal. Posts with no destination use their WordPress permalink as a legacy address.

The local review page — with its asymmetrical headline, strict grid layout with lines, warm paper texture, monospace font and coral accent — is retained as a potential visual reference for another project, without being transposed as such into the Digest.

A second local page adopts this style for the 374 posts still pending approval. It displays the detected issues and the reason for the block, offers the option to choose a destination directly or to archive the post under the WordPress permalink, and exports the decisions by merging them with the 171 existing overrides.

The review ultimately confirms that these 374 entries are not errors: multiple URLs no longer matter once the post is retained as a stand-alone editorial item. The 373 genuine posts are therefore archived under their permalink, as are the 7 posts whose external destination already existed in the Digest. Only the WordPress example is ignored, meaning 831 genuine posts out of 832 WXR publications.

A third review focuses on the 551 posts whose viewing address remains their WordPress permalink. A Brave search excluding the OOBLIK domains finds up to five public destinations per post, classifies them without publishing them and stores the responses locally. Calibration using Marion Parent’s post finds the exact portfolio ‘Deforestation & Palm Oil in Indonesia’ at the top of the list. After identity calibration — distinctive title or recognisable official domain — the complete set produces 244 top suggestions with high confidence, 265 with medium confidence, 40 with low confidence and only 2 posts with no candidates. Eight suggestions already present in the Digest are flagged to avoid duplicates. The choices remain an editorial decision which is then exported to overrides.json.

Automatic validation then retains 240 high-confidence decisions. Two pairs of entries converge on the same destination: for each, one entry adopts the retrieved link whilst the other retains its WordPress permalink. In total, 238 external destinations are thus restored without altering the catalogue’s volume: 4,836 links, 4,836 unique identifiers and no duplicate URLs. A second run of the import confirms the idempotence.

The ‘v1.15.1’ correction then re-examines all archives still attached to their permalinks, including links present in the HTML but not retained by the first validation. It restores a further 113 destinations: 8 unique explicit sources and 105 ordinary links whose identity strongly corresponds to the post. The ÉSAD Pyrénées case is thus linked directly to the current Radical Web Design page. Of the 200 remaining archives, 115 do not actually contain any external links, 6 are duplicates already present in the Digest, and only 79 still require a decision. These 79 cases are compiled at source-gap-review.html. No manual checking of the 831 entries is required. The catalogue remains at 4,836 unique URLs and identifiers.

The link taxonomy has also been streamlined on the existing tag pages . Imported or one-off variants — for example Photographes, Livre / Book or Bernard STIEGLER — are now assigned to their canonical themes. The admin panel rejects new, unregistered keywords; the WordPress importer flags them for review; and the public modal no longer generates URLs from free-form text. A catalogue check prevents any regression to a missing tag path.

The visual tweak v1.15.2 finally clarifies the source in all pop-ups. The destination, the ‘Favourites’ action and ‘Visit the site’ share a compact first line in that order. The OOBLIK Blog permalink is no longer a large, competing button: after a second adjustment, ‘Original post’ becomes a discreet secondary link. On mobile, the three main actions retain the same order, stacking neatly without overflowing.

Validation and deployment

The finalisation at v1.15.2 passes the full repository check: 148 tests of the administration service, 70 tests of the extension, verification of 4,836 URLs and unique identifiers, 813 associated Wayback archives, no unchecked dead archives, and a Hugo build with no warnings. The final modal is tested in a real browser on a computer and then at 375 pixels, with no horizontal overflow and the same order of actions.

The day saw 24 commits on main and 23 runs of the production workflow, all of which were successful. The latest workflow Deploy production published fe113a208. The version v1.15.2 was then confirmed in the public footer and in the logged-in admin area, after which the annotated tag was pushed to the commit that was actually deployed.

body.text:
Requests and exchanges

  • Repeated editorial content was to remain distinct from accidental duplicates.
  • Each new post should retain its own URN and date without overwriting the history.

  • The development blog was to be integrated into Flux as a standalone editorial section, with a chronological index, full-text viewing and RSS.
  • The legacy feed blog-ooblik was to remain strictly unchanged.
  • The index summaries had to be no more than three sentences long.
  • Each map was to feature a visual banner, reproduced as a square image in the full post, based on American posters from the 1940s and 1950s.

Decisions

  • A standard submission remains deduplicated and links to the most recent known post.
  • ‘Repost on LinkedIn’ is an explicit action that reopens the composer before requiring further confirmation.
  • The URL-based lock and the ‘submitting’ status remain unchanged in order to protect against concurrent submissions and ambiguous remote results.
  • docs/journal/YYYY-MM-DD.md files feed directly into the public pages via a Hugo content adapter. No copies of the posts are retained in content/.
  • The visual corpus is sourced from the IIIF feed of Northwestern University Libraries. Only ‘War posters, American’ dated from 1940 to 1959 and labelled ‘No Copyright – United States’ are included. Their source and attribution remain visible.

Implementation

  • Automatic migration from linkedin_publications to a historical append-only index organised by URL and date.
  • Addition of an occurrence counter to publication responses.
  • Reading of the central history upon opening the composer in order to directly activate ‘Confirm republishing’ on all workstations.
  • Replacement of the retrieval process with a repeatable editorial republishing process, with editable text and hashtags.
  • Update of public, technical and operational documentation.
  • Upgraded the site and administration version to v1.18.1 following the integration of the changes made on 25 August.
  • Addition of the ‘Digest Journal’ banner in Flux, an index by year and by month, dedicated pages with folio numbers, and a standalone RSS feed.
  • Strict validation of post titles, dates and summaries, accompanied by a consistency check between the Markdown files, the nine pages generated and the RSS feed.
  • Co-ordinated migration of the website and the administration panel to v1.21.0 for this new public feature.
  • Reproducible creation of a local corpus of one hundred WebP posters, with a metadata catalogue, attribution and an IIIF collection script.
  • Addition of banners on the index page, a square box within blog posts and an automatic check limiting each summary to three sentences.
  • Co-ordinated migration of the website and the administration system to v1.21.1.

title.text: Repeat without deleting on LinkedIn

body.text:
Requests and discussions

  • Analyse fifty GitHub links to produce a coherent compilation, rather than a list of top picks with no hierarchy.
  • Correct truncated URLs, moved repositories and duplicates present in the original list.
  • Group the resources editorially according to what they enable users to do.
  • Add archive images and LinkedIn share visuals to the published Digest.
  • Identify and then remove the floating white border that appeared between certain archive cards and moved in line with the window width.
  • Remove ‘Pinboard’ from all archive titles, without deleting the term from summaries, historical texts or posts that actually refer to it.
  • Reserve the ‘Digest — date’ format for contemporary curations and allow historical archives to bear only their date.
  • Position the navigation bar at the top of the viewport, without any top margin or border.
  • Simplify the lines on the home page: no line beneath the manifesto, a simple frame around the search bar and the date, followed by a slightly thicker bottom line.

Decisions

Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin, local repository
  • Date covered: Saturday 27 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev / UI editor projects
  • SHA at the end of the observed sequence: 488eb52 (feat(editor): persist photo layout templates)
  • KEREDIT version: 0.9.44/0.9.45 depending on the subsequent merge sequence; not recalculated to the nearest commit
  • Observed windows: 00:16:40 → 00:48:42, then 16:30:09 → 23:11:52 CEST
  • Minimum observed time: approximately 7h13+, a conservative sum of the two blocks excluding the long outage
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 587h27+ (580h14+ as at 26 June, + 7h13+ today)

Overall summary

The previous day had separated two topics that tended to get mixed up too easily: the web PDF on the one hand, the workshop print on the other. Today we return to the editor, but with the same underlying idea: a visual interface is not enough; a contract is needed.

For photo albums, the contract is beginning to take the form of templates. A template is not just a pretty layout. It is a reusable rule that specifies how many photos a page can hold, or where they fall, how a page responds to the chosen number of photos, and how automatic filling can offer something other than a bare grid.

Autofill is therefore evolving into a layout language, not just a magic button.

What has been built

Today’s commits show a fairly clear progression:

  • a1beea2 - simplifying a group of shape layers;
  • 7110d73 - adding canvas/page navigation arrows;
  • ac7c69e - widening the controls at the bottom of the editor;
  • 9e1f4bd - clarifying the page navigation controls;
  • 49331f7 - clarifying the spine and cover guides in books;
  • 3dfdd38 - add photo layout templates for books;
  • d91b738 - add sorting and spacing to auto-fill;
  • e057667 - add ‘full photo’ templates;
  • 42cbaee - make photo layout settings live;
  • 488eb52 - save photo layout templates.

The key point is the shift from static to interactive: layouts are no longer simply coded as arbitrary positions; they can now be selected, varied and saved.

Covers, double-page spreads and limits

The book project also continues to highlight that a book is not a homogeneous sequence of ordinary pages.

The front cover, inside front cover, inside back cover, spine and the pages of the inner section do not all serve the same purpose. Navigation must therefore remain clear: you can view a double-page spread, but certain areas are not editable and certain zones belong to the cover as a whole rather than to the inner section.

The guidelines for the spine and cover have been clarified to avoid a simple but dangerous misunderstanding: believing that what is visible on screen necessarily corresponds to a customer-editable page.

Autofill: the first true logic

Autofill now has two functions:

  • photo sorting;
  • page layout.

This is still a work in progress, not a final UX. But the principle is established: the client should not have to compose each page by hand to achieve a coherent album, nor should the tool impose a monotonous grid.

The “full-photo” templates add a much-needed sense of breathing space. A photo book needs dense pages, but also pages that allow a single image to stand on its own.

What this day reveals

The day highlights a clear product direction:

photos chargees -> tri -> rythme -> gabarits -> proposition de carnet

There is still a lot of UX work to be done. But the technical foundation is starting to speak the right language. Auto-fill must not be a black box; it must be a suggestion that the user can understand, modify, and dismiss without losing their flow.

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin, local repository
  • Date covered: Sunday 28 June 2026
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev following the merge of the templates project
  • SHA at the end of the observed sequence: af85675 (fix(editor): align autofill preview and empty slots)
  • KEREDIT version observed: 0.9.45
  • Time windows observed: 00:40:11 → 01:00:43, 09:41:39 → 10:00:14, then 17:23:56 → 19:09:30 CEST
  • Minimum observed duration: approximately 2h25+, conservative sum of the three blocks
  • Minimum cumulative duration since the start of the log: approximately 589h52+ (587h27+ as at 27 June, + 2h25+ today)

Overall reading

Sunday begins as a logical extension of 27 June: whilst the logbook can be filled in using templates, it can also be accompanied by a narrative intent.

But the day soon reveals a tension that will become central in the days that follow: adding functions is easy; organising their meaning is much more difficult.

The narrative assistant arrives. The templates are enhanced. Then the work immediately returns to something more down-to-earth: stabilising the hooks, making the preview reliable, aligning empty slots, and ensuring that the pop-up form doesn’t become an incomprehensible control panel.

Narrative assistant and enhanced templates

The first commits of the night set out an ambition:

  • f16e21c - to enhance the photo layout templates;
  • 911cebe - to add a narrative assistant for photo books;
  • 64449ca - clean up the content of the narrative assistant.

It’s a powerful idea: a photo book isn’t just a pile of images. It can have a rhythm, pauses, captions and a logical sequence.

But the risk is just as clear. If the wizard, the templates, the styles and the auto-fill each speak their own language, the user doesn’t save any time. They end up with added complexity.

Stabilise before expanding

The rest of the day’s discussion brings the topic back to the product level:

  • ac3e6f2 - keeping the hooks in the auto-fill modal stable;
  • b5b8581 - implement Impeccable and refine the autocomplete modal;
  • af85675 - align the autocomplete preview with the empty fields;
  • 0089b32 - release version 0.9.45.

The crucial point is the preview. A fill preview cannot be merely decorative. If it does not show the actual project, with the correct pages, the correct placements and the correct boundaries, it is misleading.

Automatic layout is therefore beginning to move beyond a simple form. It must become a visual experience: seeing the notebook, understanding what is going to be added, and being able to try a different layout.

What this day corrects in the method

The risk of over-engineering is already apparent.

There are enough building blocks to construct a powerful workflow:

  • narrative assistant;
  • templates;
  • sorting;
  • pacing;
  • number of photos per page;
  • preview;
  • filling;
  • reuse at a later stage.

But too many building blocks on display in one place create confusion. Today’s work already points in a direction that will be confirmed later: quick mode must remain quick. Technical concepts may exist in the code, but they must not all become visible options.

What this day leaves us with

The photo log is starting to take shape around two main themes:

composition automatique -> poser les photos
assistant narratif      -> proposer une lecture

These two strands are useful, but they must not be mixed too soon. The product needs internal power and external simplicity. Moving forward, the focus should be less on adding options and more on choosing which ones to hide.

Overall summary

Today’s work moves away slightly from the visible core of the editor to strengthen the tools surrounding it.

The photo log is still present with the ‘refill’ preview, but the main thread is now up and running: reducing noise, making feed testing easier, documenting upcoming editor projects, and hardening GOF in terms of security and performance.

It’s not the sort of day that yields a spectacular screenshot. It’s the sort of day that prevents the beta from becoming impossible to monitor.

KEREDIT: refill, lint and workshop command

Today’s KEREDIT commits:

  • 0aa6b31 - aligning the notebook refill preview;
  • 87d667d - restore a clean lint state;
  • a513692 - track the editor refactoring backlog;
  • 7051e75 - reduce beta observability noise;
  • a59e3a2 - added the `test-flux` command for the workshop pipeline;
  • 30ea669 - bump release 0.9.47;
  • e1d5676 - streamline the WooCommerce project recovery options.

The most important practical point is test-flux. A workshop pipeline cannot rely solely on unit tests or manual clicks. We need a command capable of replaying the WooCommerce -> KEREDIT -> GOF -> workshop flow in a reproducible manner.

The other useful point is the reduction in observability noise. Too many logs make the real signals invisible. In closed beta, we want to see the errors that change a decision, not every single system heartbeat.

WooCommerce: resuming without overloading

The WooCommerce project resumption selector has been streamlined.

This is not a cosmetic detail. In the e-commerce workflow, users often return after an interruption: an order link, a project already created, photos already present, and a decision to resume. If the resumption screen looks like a technical dashboard, trust declines.

The fix follows the same principle as the order form: less mental load, a clearer path.

GOF: security, cache and staging retention

GOF also saw significant changes that day:

  • f1341a8 - tightening access to artefacts and rendering;
  • 61e98a6 - limiting the cache buffer for PDF assets;
  • 43fdfff /e7bc345 - adding and then tightening the staging retention workflow;
  • 7adff60 - released GOF 0.1.85;
  • e38bf59 / 37b38da - added and then enlarged the GOF favicon.

The GOF hardening counts towards KEREDIT because GOF is not an annex. It is the artefacts forge: web PDFs, print PDFs, workshop files, operator verification. If GOF retains data for too long, exposes too much, or consumes too much cache space, the entire chain becomes vulnerable.

What this day leaves us with

The theme of the day is simple:

moins de bruit -> plus de diagnostic
plus de replay -> moins de superstition

KEREDIT is starting to have the tools needed to test an entire workshop workflow without having to mentally reconstruct everything every time an incident occurs. GOF is becoming stricter on security and more resource-efficient.

It’s not spectacular, but it’s exactly the sort of work that makes a beta version usable.

Overall summary

The hundredth day of the log.

This figure marks a day that is very representative of the project: the code may generate quickly, but the product doesn’t become good simply because it has lots of features. It becomes good when the user understands what’s happening, when unnecessary choices disappear, and when the interface stops creating entropy.

Today’s task focuses on filling the notebook quickly.

Initially, the workflow can do a lot of things: select pages, process the cover, add pages, sort, filter, alternate, choose styles, select templates, preview, apply. On paper, it’s powerful. In user testing, it’s too much.

So today’s task is to do the opposite of over-engineering: remove the visible options, retain the internal power, and transform the quick mode into a KISS experience.

What does KISS mean here?

KISS doesn’t mean ‘poor’.

KISS means:

  • a clear primary purpose;
  • settings that match the client’s vocabulary;
  • a preview that truly shows the notebook;
  • simple, reversible actions with no surprises;
  • technical options hidden unless they are needed to make a decision.

Quick form-filling must be guided by a simple principle:

placer mes photos dans mon carnet et me laisser essayer autre chose sans stress

Anything that forces the user to understand the engine’s internal terminology becomes suspect.

The quick workflow simplifies

The modal window is gradually reduced to just a few choices:

  • sorting photos;
  • number of pages;
  • photos per page;
  • margins;
  • spacing;
  • layout: regular, alternating, occasional full-page spreads;
  • Global action: Reorganise all;
  • local action: Reorganise on one page.

The ‘Quick’ and ‘Wizard’ buttons disappear from the header of this modal. Quick mode is now the default mode. The narrative wizard remains in the codebase, but it does not need to be displayed in this workflow until it has a clear product specification.

The main button remains result-oriented:

Placer X photos dans le carnet

This is clearer than “Start auto-fill”.

Global preview: what is seen must be what is applied

The preview becomes the centrepiece of the workflow.

It shows the notebook after simulated filling, without modifying the store until the user applies the changes. It includes existing pages, pages that have been added, the cover where included, and retains the current position when changing style or rhythm.

Several UI details have been refined:

  • the unnecessary preview counter has been removed;
  • the ‘page modified’ borders have been removed;
  • the arrows have been moved closer to the notebook;
  • the controls are grouped on the left;
  • the help section has been transformed into a reassuring, overlay panel;
  • the close button is more visible, without any unnecessary tooltips;
  • the page backgrounds before thumbnails load are replaced by a paper-like grey;
  • the sliders use a terracotta colour consistent with the buttons.

The preview is no longer just for decoration. It serves to reassure users.

Reorganise everything, then just one page

The ‘Reorganise All’ button maintains the selected layout. If the user is set to ‘regular’, it remains in ‘regular’ mode. It changes the compatible templates, not the client’s overall logic.

A major bug has been fixed: with one photo per page, the engine was still forcing full-width display. This was consistent with a previous contract, but contrary to actual usage: if the local ‘Reorganise’ button can suggest other templates for a photo, ‘Reorganise All’ must be able to do so as well.

The cover is given the same trial feature: when it contains a photo, the local ‘Reorganise’ button appears on the front cover, centred on the right-hand half, not in the middle of the spread.

Undo without creating a second editor

The Undo button becomes a mini composition history.

It retains up to 5 states, but only for:

  • ‘Reorganise All’;
  • Reorganise a page.

Manual adjustments such as margins, spacing, rhythm or photos per page reset this history. This is intentional: the aim is to undo a visual exploration, not to create a parallel history system within the modal.

Here again, KISS does not mean a lack of convenience. It is a refusal to add a mechanism whose scope the user would no longer understand.

Local seed: the trust reminder

Today’s work is also marked by the fear of losing locally stored data.

The day before, anti-seed protection was put in place. Today, the issue remains relevant: a local database intended to serve as a mirror must not be treated as a disposable database. The Zine product, visible on the VPS but absent locally, served as a very concrete reminder.

An AI tool can execute a command quickly. The project, however, requires a slow and non-negotiable rule:

ne jamais ecraser silencieusement des donnees metier vivantes

What Day 100 reveals about the project

Code generates quickly. Sometimes too quickly.

In an hour, you can get an auto-fill feature with dozens of parameters. But it then takes two days to organise the semantic and visual chaos: which words to keep, which controls to hide, which preview to trust, which action cancels what, which page is really the target, which option builds trust and which creates confusion.

Day 100 therefore does not mark a major functional expansion. It marks a discipline:

puissance interne, simplicite externe

And that is probably a good definition of KEREDIT at this stage: a ‘workshop-first’ product that must hide a great deal of complexity without deceiving the user.

WooCommerce observability incident

The Grafana alert “5xx errors > 2%” did not indicate a widespread outage. The VPS probes showed a healthy backend, and the metrics indicated that the 500 errors were concentrated on POST /api/woocommerce/webhook.

The diagnosis traced the issue back to the WooCommerce webhook 13, active on ooblik.com, topic order.updated, KEREDIT URL woo_ooblik_live. This webhook is legitimate: it links WooCommerce orders to KEREDIT. The noise stems from the native deliver_ping(), which sends a non-JSON body of the type webhook_id=13. KEREDIT expects a signed JSON order and therefore responded with a 500 status code to this ping. Genuine order webhooks continued to go through.

Operational conclusion: no global backend incident, but a fix is required. KEREDIT remains useful for handling this ping via 200 or by rejecting it, without cluttering up the 5xx alerts.

Moving forward

There are two points to bear in mind:

  • check in the editor that snapping, guides and multi-block alignment remain user-friendly, not just covered by tests.
