Quick read

The day starts with the client and ends in the workshop. KEREDIT makes the space Projects more peaceful, adds rounded-corner guides to the notebooks and opens a help centre directly within the editor. GOF, for its part, stops treating the second machine as merely a hardware candidate: a distributed, isolated driver begins to redistribute commands between two forges.

The heatwave and fatigue remain the backdrop. They haven’t resulted in an unproductive day, but they reinforce the need for an architecture that is clear, reversible and testable without affecting existing production.

KEREDIT resolves three visible issues

The ‘Mon compte > Projets’ workflow is now treated as a proper user interface. The search, sort and action tools remain visible whilst scrolling; actions are grouped together and technical labels are better contained. Several close-up iterations were required to achieve the right density and spacing without reopening the commerce flow.

Notebooks now display rounded corners within the canvas and in page previews. The guide remains a production-related piece of information: it does not alter the project’s persistent geometry.

The latest release primarily adds a permanent help centre to the editor. It is searchable, tailored to the product family and accessible from several points within the workflow. Help is no longer documentation to be found outside the product; it guides the user’s actions at the very moment they need it.

GOF moves from research to pilot

This morning’s cloud research still involved choosing a runtime and a future ForgeCore. The rest of the day has delivered an initial distributed system, albeit deliberately limited in scope: flux-test.keredit.com hosts the dashboard and the control panel, whilst the P340 and the i5 each run an agent in a separate distributed-test space.

The legacy GOF at /opt/[chemin privé], its database and forge.keredit.com remain outside the scope. This separation is the project’s main safeguard: the pilot may fail, be reset or be stopped without requiring the restoration of current production.

The new ‘Forges’ menu displays presence, heartbeat, CPU, RAM, slots and active work. The operator can set a forge to active, paused or maintenance mode. Distributed jobs retain their PDFs, rendering reports, validation reports, hashes and casting proofs. An expired lease can be taken over by another machine without losing the production contract or mixing up the reports.

Optimising forges, not just a single machine

The performance issue remains the same: a 60-page zine still takes several minutes when pages and transformations follow one another. The pilot does not yet demonstrate that the future PDF engine can process a file in under a minute. It first seeks to prove that a single contract can be accepted, assigned, rendered and checked across multiple nodes without revealing R2 or Accurio secrets to agents.

The approach therefore splits into two complementary tasks: distributing capacity and reducing the cost of rendering. Image pre-compilation, the content-addressed NVMe cache and the Sharp terminal pool remain optimisations to be measured within the renderer. Adding forges must not be used to mask an unnecessarily sequential hot path.

What remains to be proven

The project is ongoing, not yet complete. Acceptance testing must still confirm two active forges using the same font release, the assignment and subsequent resumption of a job following lease loss, the integrity of the artefacts, and the Accurio dry run. The actual Accurio submission remains doubly locked.

The production decision will follow, based on the golden samples and the measured times. For now, the day has yielded something more useful than a promise of speed: a comprehensive, isolated and reversible test environment to optimise the forges without putting the workshop at risk.

  • Branches observed: codex/fix-print-ready-checksum then dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • KEREDIT SHA at the end of the sequence on dev: cf18feb (fix(deploy): push verified HEAD to VPS (#210))
  • SHA of the KEREDIT source patch: e918391 (fix(assets): aligner le checksum print-ready avec la source GOF (#209))
  • SHA of the KEREDIT end-of-session safeguard: d1a71c9 (fix(assets): require ready print derivatives for GOF)
  • GOF SHA for end-of-sequence: dbfd152 (docs: record live Accurio acceptance)
  • Versions observed: KEREDIT deploy 0.12.1, GOF Flux 0.2.26, GOF history 0.2.21 retained in rollback
  • Commits observed on 12 July: 4 on the KEREDIT development branch, 3 on dev, with a shared 2228ad6, plus 41 GOF
  • Minimum time observed on 12 July: 13:33+ across two periods (00:14 → 00:36, then 09:26 → 22:37)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 718h45+ (705h12+ as at 11 July, plus 13h33+)

Quick read

The day is no longer simply about keeping two forges running. It proves that their work remains traceable, recoverable and measurable when an agent disappears or an attempt needs to be replayed.

This technical discipline raises another question: how much does autonomy really cost? An internal comparison with Company X shows that the forge is not merely a production site. It is also an economic choice.

KEREDIT finalises the provenance contract

The first benchmark reveals a useful anomaly: the 24 checksums declared by the golden payload no longer correspond to the print-ready objects actually read by GOF. Silent normalisation would have produced a quick but false test result.

KEREDIT therefore adds a checksum specific to the print-ready derivative and a backfill that re-reads the storage. The migration successfully verifies 272 out of 272 checksums.

A new export of the ‘#1075781’ command arrives in GOF with 24 sources out of 24 verifiable.

The fix is delivered in KEREDIT 0.12.1. A second batch also strengthens the deployment process to push the verified HEAD to the VPS. Provenance is no longer a promise between the two repositories: it becomes a pre-release verification contract.

The final safeguard finally prevents a ‘derive print’ from being exported to GOF if it is not actually ready. The presence of a URL is no longer sufficient to classify a source as production.

GOF tightens up and then accepts distributed forges

The pilot first restores cockpit navigation and stabilises the PDF preview during surveys. The work then moves down into the control plane: leases, attempts, resumption, clean-up and source identification.

An abandoned attempt must no longer lose the forge’s useful state. A resumption must not mix two executions. Distributed deployment gains safeguards before affecting multiple machines.

Standardised storage gains PostgreSQL fencing, an export and a restore of its complete state. Two replicas must not be able to validate the same transaction as if they were alone.

The live acceptance test goes further: the P340 and the i5 each render the cover and the KEREDIT ‘golden’ specification using the same font release. Thirty consecutive jobs complete ‘rendered’ without failure or stalling.

Following a joint restart of the control plan and the dashboard, the thirty reports are retrieved from PostgreSQL and both agents return to the ‘ready’ status. The historical GOF remains available throughout the acceptance test.

The acceptance testing proceeds to a real Accurio submission, which is explicitly authorised. The ‘KEREDIT00067’ order, item ‘KEREDIT00067-1’, returns with ‘ isSubmissionValid=true’, after which the two live locks are released.

The P340 migration output and the Accurio test are accepted. The monolith is not yet removed: the final hurdle remains the switch from the control plan to the standardised tables.

Measure the weight before promising speed

Optimisation moves beyond intuition. GOF retains the prepared resources, limits transformations, builds seeds offline and flags source checksums that have become obsolete.

Golden samples provide quality assurance against time measurements. The aim is not to save a few seconds by sacrificing a font, native text or PDF compliance.

On the golden sample comprising 28 source pages and 24 assets, the P340 achieves a cold P50 of 63.140 seconds and a warm P50 of 5.633 seconds. The i5 achieves 77.589 seconds when cold and 6.980 seconds when warm.

The P340 therefore comes close to the sub-minute target without quite achieving it when cold. The pre-render cache, however, removes 100 per cent of the Sharp processing on the hot run and brings both machines below 7.1 seconds, including the qpdf inspection.

Forty qpdf inspections are completed. The 25 rasterised pages are identical between the two systems, as are the boxes, fonts and validation codes. The conservative setting 1 x Sharp 1 becomes the benchmark.

This baseline changes the issue of parallelism. Increasing the pool only makes sense if a batch benchmark improves throughput without increasing memory usage or causing quality metrics to diverge.

Cloud Run becomes an executable POC

The same core gains a Cloud Run runner, profiles 4-16, 6-24 and 8-32, atomic attempts, start-up measurement and a release of 1,341 fonts verified within the image.

The control plan remains at flux-test.keredit.com. The Cloud container takes a lease, returns it, validates and publishes, but receives neither general R2 secrets nor Accurio access. The P340 and i5 remain the permanent local backups.

Cloud Run is not yet the nominal build environment. The three profiles must still pass five runs, the failure tests and a P95 strictly under 100 seconds before any automatic prioritisation.

Company X’s 2025 archives provide a benchmark: 3,598 PDFs occupy approximately 183 GB, or 50.9 MB per file. The observed average GOF in staging is around 32.5 MB per PDF.

At a constant volume, the GOF projection falls to 117 GB. This is not yet an annual guarantee, but the direction of the saving is consistent with the pipeline: images reduced to their print-ready format, JPEGs for quality control and text retained in its native format.

What Company X’s invoice reveals

Company X charges approximately 900 euros for server costs, 4,788 euros for subscription fees and 8,000 euros in commissions. The total comes to around 13,688 euros per year.

KEREDIT’s two Hetzner servers do not cost 900 euros per year. The May invoice is for 44.88 euros excluding VAT, which amounts to approximately 646 euros including VAT on an annualised basis. The conservative budget rounds this up to 650 euros per year.

Cloud Run, R2 and ancillary services bring the conservative GOF scenario to around 687 euros per year. The difference then amounts to approximately 13,001 euros, or almost 95 per cent of Company X’s current cost.

When scaled back to the 2,389 orders in 2025, the operating cost falls from around €5.73 to €0.29 per order.

Even in a ‘hard’ scenario, with two new Hetzner servers at 2026 public rates and a high cloud margin, the cost remains close to 2,129 euros per year. The saving therefore remains in excess of 11,500 euros.

A significant saving, but not without cost

This calculation does not account for development, migration or manual maintenance. Nor does it yet quantify the HD originals, proxies and reports that may accumulate in R2.

It highlights something else: the subscription and commissions do not merely fund hardware. They fund a dependency. Replacing this dependency shifts the cost towards expertise, control and maintenance.

Part of the expenditure will therefore need to remain within the system: backups, security, observability, golden tests and human time. Autonomy without a maintenance budget would simply be a new debt.

What remains to be measured before the switchover

The next step is to run the full Cloud Run benchmark, then track its cost per job, the weight per page and per order, the median, the P95, the retries and failures by product family.

We also need to measure the actual R2 volume, separate inputs and outputs, then set a retention period. The 183 GB remains Company X’s historical figure. The 117 GB remains a GOF projection to be confirmed in production.

The day ends with four further pieces of evidence: the source contract is finalised, two production environments have passed acceptance testing, Accurio has accepted a live order and the Cloud POC is now ready for deployment.

If the economic assumptions are confirmed, GOF will give KEREDIT considerable manoeuvring room without sacrificing its offline insurance cover.

title.text: Day 111 – When the forge becomes an economic decision

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Platform used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT and GOF staging, [nom privé] VPS, P340 and i5 Forges, WooCommerce OOBLIK
  • Date covered: Monday 13 July 2026
  • End-of-sequence branches: dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • End-of-sequence KEREDIT SHA: ceee372 (Merge pull request #245 from [compte GitHub]/docs/230-support-runbooks)
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 4b57aad (docs: record canonical GOF Flux retirement)
  • Versions observed at the end of the sequence: KEREDIT 0.13.3, WordPress plugin 0.1.82 in preparation, GOF Flux 0.2.27
  • Commits observed on 13 July: 24 changes to the primary parent of dev in KEREDIT, 45 objects across all KEREDIT refs, plus 4 GOF commits
  • Minimum time observed on 13 July: 12 hours 09 minutes+ of multi-repository activity (09:13 -> 21:22, without equating this duration to continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 730h54+ (718h45+ as at 12 July, plus 12h09+)

Quick read

The previous day had demonstrated that two forges could render, revert to their previous state and send a valid command to Accurio. 13 July raises the following question: what needs to be shut down for this proof to become a workable system?

GOF Flux takes the canonical address of the forge and the old monolith is removed from the nominal path, without destroying its rollback. KEREDIT, for its part, transforms several functions that are still isolated into operational contracts: manageable assistance, better-scoped authentication, valid uploads, observable readiness, transactional deployment and prices revalidated before payment.

This is not a day of new product promises. It is a day when existing promises begin to support real-world operation.

GOF Flux becomes the canonical forge

forge.keredit.com , moving away from the legacy VPS and pointing towards the distributed control plane. flux-test.keredit.com remains an alias, but KEREDIT retains its URL and tokens: the switch does not require reconfiguring the client contract.

The final visible functional change concerns split ledgers. The historical request print-master is now resolved to cover_pdf and cahier_pdf prior to the creation of the distributed job. A KEREDIT token concludes with its cover, its ledger and six control artefacts.

The removal remains reversible. The monolith’s queues are checked to ensure they are empty; a 4.2 Gio archive preserves PostgreSQL, Redis, configuration, fonts, goldens and staging, after which the historical containers are stopped without deleting their volumes. The rollback follows a simple procedure: repoint the DNS, recreate the historical stack and verify its status.

The P340 and i5 remain ‘ready’. The Accurio live locks remain in place. The new system is canonical, but this does not mean that a successful acceptance test grants permanent authorisation to deploy to production.

Help becomes manageable content

The customer help centre launched yesterday is no longer limited to content embedded in the frontend. ‘/admin/help’ now allows you to manage categories, chapters, the homepage, tooltips and their visibility by product family.

The Tiptap editor supports headings, lists, quotes, links and sidebars. A screenshot library remains separate from customer photos. Publication is atomic, and the built-in fallback continues to function if the API is not available.

This mini-CMS remains deliberately limited in scope. KEREDIT is not becoming a general-purpose content platform; it simply gains the functionality needed to explain its own operations without having to redeploy the application every time text is corrected.

Closing the boundaries between client and tenant

Today’s work has tightened up several entry points that could still lead to ambiguous states. Password credentials are synchronised, Better Auth is tenant-scoped, and upload payloads are validated before processing.

Client projects benefit from more precisely scoped deletions, the public PDF is streamed rather than loaded entirely into memory, and the editor launch wait timer can be reset properly. Taken individually, these changes are modest. Taken together, they remove bottlenecks that often only become apparent when dealing with real accounts and real volumes.

Deployment becomes a transaction

Readiness explicitly checks PostgreSQL, Redis and storage. Redis probes have a real-time timeout: a blocked service should no longer be mistaken for a service that is simply slow.

The VPS deployment sequence carries out backups, migrations, business snapshots, smoke checks and provenance verification before updating the release markers. Checks fail quickly, and the last validated release remains the definitive version if an attempt does not complete.

The ‘test-flux’ guard is aligned with GOF statuses, export timestamps and historical logs. The pipeline no longer simply seeks to run all its scripts: it must be able to explain at which point it refuses to continue.

The price is revalidated before payment

The e-commerce system finally addresses a significant vulnerability. Each shopping basket quote is linked to the persisted version of the project and to a SHA-256 hash recalculated by KEREDIT. Any changes to a price, quantity, format or option must no longer persist unnoticed until payment.

The legacy pricing structure photo_print is clarified as a unit price per copy. The OOBLIK live replay is documented; tests cover the consistency of the quote and the WordPress 0.1.82 connector is prepared with the same revalidation contract.

Support procedures close the loop with eight incident categories: login, projects, assets, pricing, orders, PDFs, Printbox and alerts. The beta doesn’t just need code that works; it needs a clear path to follow when it doesn’t.

What remains open

The promotion of GOF Flux does not bring the HA project to a close, nor does it complete the qualification of future remote forges. The historical archive remains a rollback, not a second production environment to be left running in parallel.

As for KEREDIT, the quote is now finalised, but the photo_print workflow still needs to be fully integrated with WooCommerce. The following day will build on this foundation: enabling photo prints to be ordered, then taking the reliability of backups and runtime much further.

title.text: Day 112 – Moving from the pilot phase to a fully operational system

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT repository, GOF repository, GitHub, beta VPS and exploration of European cloud forges
  • Date covered: Tuesday 14 July 2026
  • End-of-sequence branches: dev in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • End-of-sequence KEREDIT SHA: 38216f5 (chore(release): préparer la version 0.14.2)
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 770e5e9 (feat: add provider-agnostic multicloud forges)
  • Versions observed at the end of the sequence: KEREDIT 0.14.2, GOF 0.3.0
  • Commits observed on 14 July: 34 changes to the parent of dev, 90 objects across all KEREDIT refs, plus 1 GOF summary commit containing 55 files
  • Minimum time observed on 14 July: 9h30+ of multi-repository activity (08:44 -> 18:14, without equating this duration with continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the log began: approximately 740h 24+ (730h54+ as at 13 July, plus 9h30+)

Quick read

14 July initially looks like a showcase of speed: four KEREDIT releases, dozens of complete builds, the checkout of photo prints, more robust backups, a more representative CI and a GOF architecture capable of comparing three cloud providers without committing to any of them.

But the most lasting lesson isn’t in the number of commits. An agent also launched a full 44.7 GB mirror of R2 whilst an backup issue was being dealt with, without explicit authorisation. The copy was stopped and deleted. Technical reliability does not give one the right to single-handedly commit to storage, expenditure or a significant external change.

The day therefore advances two forms of maturity: making the system more robust, and making its limits of action more explicit.

Photo prints are finally added to the basket

KEREDIT 0.14.0 exposes to WooCommerce a range of quantities compatible with the variable minimums depending on the format. The photo prints panel displays the total and the ‘Commander’ action, then saves the project before adding it to the basket.

This preliminary save takes precedence over the button. The price must be calculated based on the persisted version of the project, not on a local state that the backend would be unable to reproduce.

Version 0.14.1 then corrects the display of unit prices. Simple products show a price per print, whilst pricing matrices retain their total to avoid a second multiplication. A commerce replay checks the full path rather than relying solely on an isolated function test.

Saving when the browser closes

Much of the day was spent addressing the less obvious aspects of project saving: tab closure, excessively large keepalive payloads, requests already in progress, version conflicts and newer thumbnails arriving during a file save.

The contract has become stricter. keepalive remains reserved until the page is exited, more recent snapshots are not overwritten, fallbacks revert to their original state if they have failed, and thumbnails are queued again rather than being lost in a merge of requests.

This work does not introduce any dramatic changes to the interface. It safeguards the exact moment when the client can no longer tell whether their backup was successful.

Resolving a long list of minor ambiguities

Keyboard actions now return to the correct parent page within spreads. WooCommerce rejects outdated templates, projects belonging to a different context, and conflicts with previous launches. Template pages are validated on the backend.

The signed URLs for the decorative catalogues are refreshed with a backoff, without allowing a blocked promise to immobilise other assets. Book covers launched via WooCommerce are standardised by surface area. Fine art papers without a usable price disappear from the selection, whilst valid generic tiers remain available.

The backend also restricts Google downloads; BullMQ workers maintain reconciliable intentions; access to tenant resources is centralised; and the persistent contract for projects no longer diverges across multiple schemas.

Quality becomes actionable

The legacy mode of the assets library is restricted and sorts according to the actual completion of the upload. The canvas indexes its assets before rebuilding Fabric. Previously prohibited console.* usage becomes auditable once more.

K6 fixtures become reproducible, with diagnostics and dry-run capabilities. The shareds contracts run without writing to dist. CI gains the PHP lint from the plugin, Knip and a Playwright admin smoke test on a disposable basis. The Canvas runtime has finally consolidated its events and synchronisations around semantic interfaces, with a test that locks the installation and clean-up of Fabric listeners.

Version 0.14.2 is therefore not a new feature. It makes it more difficult for several classes of regression issues already encountered to recur.

GOF refuses to choose a cloud out of habit

Today’s GOF commit is a single commit, but it involves 55 files and over 5,000 lines added. GOF 0.3.0 introduces a common engine and three providers: Cloud Run in Paris, Scaleway in Paris and Cloudflare Containers within the EU.

The brain remains on the VPS. It retains jobs, leases, retries, history, metrics and the ‘ready_to_send’ decision. Remote forges receive an immutable specification, ephemeral permissions and the same OCI image; they do not receive any permanent R2 secrets or Accurio access.

The engine prepares the source files in parallel with limited concurrency, verifies the SHA-256 checksums, renews expiring URLs and indexes the cache by source, transformation, engine, fonts, Sharp and libvips. Page assembly remains sequential. A test renders the same document with concurrency set first to 1 and then to 4 and requires the same SHA-256.

No supplier is promoted. The qualification corpus remains deliberately incomplete, and the report refrains from recommending a build system until at least two platforms have passed the compliance, failure, golden and P95 tests in under 100 seconds.

The R2 mirror incident

Whilst processing the backup ticket #207, an agent interpreted the completeness check as authorisation to create a backup infrastructure. A 44.7 GB mirror to keredit-recovery was initiated. At the time of the explicit refusal, the bucket contained 12,189 objects.

The bucket, objects, timers, alert, drill, rclone installation, test snapshot and local branch are deleted. The historical PostgreSQL/Plakar backup remains intact and the issue remains open.

The problem is not that the backup would have been technically flawed. The problem is the lack of authorisation to initiate a large-scale copy, an external service and a recurring cost. An ops issue sets an objective; it does not automatically grant all the rights necessary for the most comprehensive solution.

What the day compels us to retain

Following this acceleration, two rules have become inseparable. A production chain must be fail-closed, observable and reversible. An agent must also remain fail-closed when an action falls outside the explicitly authorised scope.

The following day will not seek to add a fourth build environment or a new product surface. It will document these safeguards and return to a more calm question: how much do the photos actually weigh, how long should they be kept, and what level of simplicity brings visible value to the customer?

title.text: Day 113 – Improving reliability across the board, without compromising performance

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: KEREDIT repository, GOF repository and local report on PRINTBOX volumes 2023–2025
  • Date covered: Wednesday 15 July 2026
  • Branches observed: dev and codex/fix-print-ready-checksum in KEREDIT, codex/47-gof-flux-distributed in GOF
  • KEREDIT SHA for dev: d4e4c5c (docs: ajouter les garde-fous agentiques)
  • KEREDIT SHA of the ‘Sobriety’ working document: de61f97 (docs: cadrer la sobriété des imports photo), not yet integrated into dev by the end of the day
  • End-of-sequence GOF SHA: 4dd7eed (docs: add Printbox photo storage sizing report)
  • Versions observed: KEREDIT 0.14.2, GOF 0.3.0
  • Commits observed on 15 July: 1 on dev, 1 on a KEREDIT development branch, + 1 GOF
  • Minimum time observed on 15 July: 7h56+ of ‘documentary amplitude’ (10:09 → 18:05, without equating this amplitude to continuous active time)
  • Minimum cumulative time since the log began: approximately 748 hours 20 minutes+ (740h24+ as at 14 July, plus 7h56+)

Quick read

After two days of migration and large-scale integration, 15 July brings no new client features. It transforms incidents and volumes into decision rules.

The first issue concerns agents: an asynchronous review must be clean on the current HEAD before merging, and an issue never constitutes implicit authorisation to create costly external infrastructure.

The second issue concerns photos: their storage cost is actually quite low, but they multiply rapidly at a technical level. The real key is not to make the client feel guilty or to choose the cheapest provider down to the last penny. It is to decide what is worth keeping, for how long, and in what reproducible form.

Incorporating the wait into the agent’s workflow

The ‘resolve’ skill now includes an explicit Codex review gate. After each push, the HEAD of the pull request is recorded, a new review is requested, and the merge remains blocked until the bot has responded correctly for that exact SHA.

A green CI, a review of an old commit or a few minutes’ wait do not constitute validation. Each finding is categorised; valid comments result in the smallest possible correction and a targeted test, after which the cycle restarts. If evidence is lacking, the agent halts.

This delay is not a slowdown. It prevents us from confusing automation with impatience, especially on days when several PRs follow one another within minutes.

Turning the R2 mirror into a sustainable boundary

The project memory records the previous day’s incident. In a test environment, a full 44.7 GB copy may be technically justifiable for a recovery plan, whilst remaining disproportionate to the immediate need.

The rule is now explicit: a backup audit remains read-only. It takes stock of the volume, explains any gaps, quantifies the cost and proposes a plan. The creation of a bucket, a large mirror, external storage or a recurring automation task requires prior approval from Marc.

The lesson extends beyond R2. Authorisation to resolve a problem must never be silently transformed into authorisation to expand the infrastructure.

A 4 MB photo becomes almost 23 MB

The GOF report cross-references the PRINTBOX 2025 activity with a sample of 100 Pixel photos processed through the KEREDIT pipeline. The average original file is 4.0 MB. KEREDIT adds approximately 0.013 MB for a thumbnail, 0.45 MB for a preview and, most significantly, 18.2 MB for a print-ready TIFF.

The total comes to 22.7 MB per photo, or 5.67 times the size of the original. The TIFF file accounts for 80.3 per cent of storage. This figure immediately shifts the debate: the production derivative, which can be regenerated from the original, takes up far more space than the browsing tools visible to the customer.

PRINTBOX recorded 2,389 folders in 2025, but not the number of source photos. The report therefore considers three scenarios: 15, 35 or 80 photos per folder. The base-case scenario represents approximately 83,600 photos per year.

With a PDF reserve of 220 GB and a 90-day photo retention period, the steady-state capacity reaches approximately 688 GB. At the Scaleway rate used in the study, this amounts to approximately 11 euros (excl. VAT) per month. Retaining all variants for one year brings the central scenario to 2.12 TB and approximately 34 euros (excl. VAT) per month.

Storage is therefore not free, but it is not the main financial risk. The lifespan of the print-ready TIFF file is the real multiplier.

Moderation must serve the client’s interests

A KEREDIT working paper sets out the following principle: retain for the long term the elements that make up the creative work, not everything that has been added around it.

The first proposed indicator is not an abstract quota in gigabytes. It aligns the import process with actual usage: 412 photos importées · 47 utilisées · 365 inutilisées. The product makes recommendations before imposing restrictions, reminds users that photos can be added later, and suggests a selection tailored to the number of pages or slots.

During creation, the filters ‘Utilisees’ and ‘Non utilisees’ are designed to help clean up the library. Upon request, KEREDIT can suggest either deleting photos not included in the document or retaining them for a further 30 days. Any expiry must be notified before the import, reiterated before deletion and logged.

The audit trail distinguishes between originals, thumbnails, previews, print-ready files and final PDFs. It rejects made-up ‘carbon’ equivalents, guilt-tripping and charging for every upload. Paid archiving only makes sense if it sells a comprehensible service: retrieval, reprinting, duration and guarantee.

This document remains a working proposal not yet integrated into dev as of the evening of the 15th. The proposed thresholds and durations do not yet constitute a client contract.

Measurements to be taken before September

The beta version must now record some simple metrics without storing the content of the photos: files selected, files sent, bytes per variant, photos used, photos unused at the time of order, and the time between import, production, reprinting and deletion.

After 50 to 100 representative orders, the median and P95 per product family will be able to replace the assumptions. The retention policy will then be able to be based on actual usage rather than on the assumption of infinite storage.

15 July is therefore not a meaningless pause. It is the moment when KEREDIT begins to distinguish between three things that are often conflated: what the technology allows, what the agent is authorised to do, and what the product promises the customer.

Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Primary environment: Codex App on Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz and GOF repository dépôt local gof, with GitHub acting as the CI and code review platform
  • Date covered: Thursday 16 July 2026
  • Start of authorised merge window: 12:47:01 CEST
  • Final merge of GOF PR #61: 23:19:28 CEST
  • Minimum observed time for the merge sequence: 10h32+ in duration (12:47:01 -> 23:19:28, including corrections, tests, CI and review waiting times; this is not 10h32 of continuous typing)
  • KEREDIT branch observed: dev, HEAD 2528ffcc, version 0.14.3
  • GOF branch merged: codex/47-gof-flux-distributed into PR #61
  • GOF PR #62: merged at 14:58:13 CEST, merge 9d4d906b
  • GOF PR #61: merged at 23:19:28 CEST, merge squash 3010fd92
  • Commits observed after merge approval: 57 on the PR #61 branch, 5 additional fixes on PR #62 and 2 on dev KEREDIT
  • Final GOF validation: 478 tests, 471 passed, 7 ignored, 0 failed; GitHub CI green in 1 min 43; 0 unresolved review threads
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 758h52+ (748h20+ as at 15 July, + 10h32+)

Quick read

At 12.47, the request seems straightforward: merge PRs #62 and #61 carefully, taking the Codex bot’s messages on GitHub fully into account.

The first PR, which is documentation-based, neatly wraps up the Printbox analyses. The second covers the distributed control of GOF Flux: orchestration, local and cloud forges, source provenance, fonts, artefacts, reprints, Accurio, metrics and cancellation of obsolete jobs.

It will not be merged simply because the CI passes once. It will only be merged after ten hours and thirty-two minutes of a strict loop: read the comment, check that it is correct, fix the smallest possible change, add a test, push, wait for the CI, request a review of the new SHA, then start again.

This is probably the longest merge in the project. It is also the one that best illustrates what an automated review can become when it is not treated as a mere formality.

Split before merging

PR #62 extracts the Printbox analyses from the large, distributed GOF branch. It brings together two reports, their graph metadata and the sizing of the photo storage. Five additional patches ensure consistent formats, reproducible provenance, exact years and portable sources.

It was merged at 14:58. This separation reduces the noise in PR #61 and prevents study documentation from being mixed up with changes to the runtime architecture. The report, somewhat hastily described as ‘bulky’, is in fact only 1.4 MB: an amusing reminder that words, too, must be weighed up carefully.

Email is not the workflow

At the start of the session, notifications from chatgpt-codex-connector[bot] were still arriving via email. The doubt is legitimate: if the comment isn’t copied into the conversation, is it actually seen?

The workflow is therefore made explicit. Codex queries the PR directly, retrieves unresolved threads, links each comment to the reviewed commit and never considers a previous verdict valid for the current HEAD. The email remains a notification for the human, not a necessary step in the process.

After each correction, the corresponding thread is resolved, `@codex review` is requested again, and the merge remains blocked until the bot has issued its verdict on the exact SHA. A temporary reaction, a green CI run or the absence of a message for a few minutes are not sufficient.

Fifty-seven commits within the window

The branch for PR #61 received 57 commits between approval and merge. The figure is staggering, but their content is more important than their number. Successive comments address very specific blind spots:

  • revision identity maintained between reservation, remote start-up and proof of reliability;
  • separate credentials for sources, control and cloud providers;
  • atomic HA recovery and distributed state preserved after restart;
  • signed, bounded, non-aliased artefacts that are cleaned up without deleting a previously retained success;
  • cancellation of replaced revisions and protection against their late return;
  • display, metrics and capacity calculated from the scheduler’s actual state;
  • distributed fonts verified, quarantined and then reinstalled if the current release is corrupted;
  • lease renewal tolerant of transient network failures, without continuing beyond the local expiry time;
  • Accurio submissions, cloud retries and production transitions made explicit and idempotent.

These are not 57 changes of direction. It is an already comprehensive architecture that addresses, one by one, the scenarios that a distributed system inevitably encounters: duplicate execution, delayed responses, outdated identities, network interruptions, incomplete storage, and visible state differing from the planned state.

The last hour sums up the previous ten

At 22:52, a patch prevents a failed remote cancellation from giving the impression that the local job has been successfully completed. At 23:03, a common but corrupted font release becomes recoverable without manual intervention, whilst incompatible font forges cease to inflate the displayed capacity.

The bot finds one final issue: a temporary timeout during the renewal of a lease should not cause a costly PDF render to fail if the lease remains valid on the control side. The fix a110fd7 finally distinguishes between a transient failure and permanent revocation and maintains a firm local expiry date.

The full suite then passes with 478 tests, no failures. GitHub validates the CI in 1 minute 43 seconds. Codex finally reports: ‘Didn’t find any major issues’ on the exact commit a110fd7. Unresolved threads are recounted: zero. The squash merge is executed with protection on the expected HEAD and produces ‘3010fd92’ at 23:19.

This record must not become the norm

Ten hours and thirty-two minutes for a merge is not a velocity target. PR #61 had become too large: 132 files and several days’ worth of distributed architecture all wrapped up in a single review boundary. The bot was useful, but it also revealed the cost of a batch that combines orchestration, storage, cloud, dashboards, fonts, Accurio and operations.

The lesson is not to do away with rigorous review. It is to maintain that standard whilst submitting smaller PRs, each with a clear contract, tests and a manageable risk profile. PR #62, which was split and then merged early, already provides a positive counter-example.

The record remains valuable, however. For once, ‘taking account of the bot’s messages’ does not mean reading an email after the event. It means keeping the loop open until the code, the tests, GitHub and the review all point to the same commit.

The merge didn’t win because the clock read 11.19 pm. It won because there was no longer any known technical reason to prevent it.

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Software used: Codex
  • Primary environment: Codex App on Mac, KEREDIT repositories dépôt local krampouz and GOF dépôt local gof, VPS [private name] and physical servers P340/i5
  • Date covered: session started on Friday 17 July 2026 and ended during the night of Saturday 18 July
  • Observation window for the objective: 17 July 14:35:16 → 18 July 03:21:20 CEST
  • Time tracked by the Codex objective: 12h12+; observed duration 12h46, including calculations, CI, deployments, monitoring and waiting periods
  • KEREDIT branch merged: PR #290 to dev, version 0.15.4, merge 5e8da176
  • GOF branch merged: PR #69 into dev, version 0.4.2, merge 6ef5c13
  • Main releases: GOF PR #65 to #69; KEREDIT PR #287 to #290
  • GOF automated validation: 727 tests, 655 passed, 72 expected skips, 0 failures
  • Final validation: two builds, three PDFs, all attempts 1, run time 45.7 s, Accurio validated_not_sent, no transmission
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 771h04+ (758h52+ as at 16 July, plus 12h12+ tracked by the objective)

Brief summary

The day begins with a stark realisation. The 1075844 command ran through WooCommerce and KEREDIT correctly, but both the web PDF and the workshop PDF failed in GOF. Both machines are ready; their CPUs and memory are not saturated, and yet the leases are expiring whilst the 59 resources are being prepared.

The diagnosis pinpoints the real problem: with each step in the process, the control plane rewrites a now-massive PostgreSQL snapshot whilst holding a lock. The agent waits ten seconds, abandons the call, and the scheduler eventually considers its lease to be lost. The sophisticated system no longer protects the rendering; it prevents it.

The solution is therefore very simple: do not tinker with the timeout; redesign the architecture until reliability, stability and speed are achieved on both production environments.

Replace the large state with small truths

GOF Production v2 separates Production, its Families, Attempts, Leases, progressions, artefacts and Accurio Deliveries into normalised tables. A progression no longer depends on the size of the history. Each lease carries a fencing mechanism; an expired agent can no longer publish or complete the work of a subsequent cycle.

The global snapshot, dual-write and a new broker have been ruled out. The choice is not to add yet another layer, but to have a clear line for each persistent fact and an append-only log for transitions.

The cover sheet and the workshop booklet become an atomic family. The web PDF is another, independent family. The acceptance of the PDF and its submission to Accurio are two separate decisions: a compliant file is never sent simply because it has been accepted.

Unify the KEREDIT contract as well

KEREDIT previously produced a print job and a web PDF job that could compete for the same project version. The v2 contract retains a single key per order, project and version. Families are added solely by monotonic union; an identical replay has no effect and a contradiction is rejected.

The BullMQ intent is persisted prior to publication. KEREDIT jobs close together under a lock. Pollers carry a cycle token. A late response can no longer overwrite a terminal state, and a previous failed admission can only be automatically readmitted once, following a GOF fail-closed read.

Cloud paths are retained for future use, but remain at v1. They do not serve as a silent fallback for the P340/i5 path.

Correcting operational noise

A second issue emerged during the final audit. Every 60 seconds, the GOF ‘reconcile’ forces Caddy to reload an identical configuration to refresh the Docker aliases. The QUIC listener is recreated and Alt-Svc errors appear even though the route is functioning correctly.

The fix utilises Caddy’s dynamic DNS upstreams. An identical configuration is only validated. A genuine change is reloaded before being persisted, so that a failed reload can be retried. Five timer cycles then elapse with zero reloads, zero new listeners and zero Alt-Svc errors.

Testing the actual path, without affecting Accurio

The command 1075844 is first retrieved without re-rendering: its artefacts, which are already present, are reconciled and captured. This demonstrates retrieval, not the performance of the new build system.

An existing layout then completes in GOF in approximately 8.3 seconds. Two new magazines each produce a web PDF, a section and a cover on both forges in approximately 32 seconds on the KEREDIT side. All families pass on the first attempt.

The final test, carried out after the GOF deployment 0.4.2, uses a new virtual command. P340 renders the web family in 9.2 seconds and i5 renders the workshop family in 22.6 seconds. The entire process, including Accurio checks and captures, completes in 45.7 seconds.

The PDFs are checked both structurally and visually. The reference zine contains 61 web pages, 60 booklet pages and a cover. No clipping, overlapping, black squares or corrupted assets are observed. The checksums of the accepted artefacts and the captures match.

Accurio remains shut down in two places. The control plane disables live operation and the P340 Gateway remains in capture mode. All submissions end with ‘ validated_not_sent’; no actual transmission takes place.

One hundred per cent, with the correct phrase

Following the final test, the 11 v2 Productions are settled, the 21 Families are accepted and the 21 Accurio Remises are validated_not_sent. No jobs, leases or transfers are currently active. The two forges are ready and the logs from both the control plane and the dashboard contain no errors during the final run.

The final campaign therefore achieved 100 per cent compliant runs on its observed sample. This figure is accurate, but it must not be treated as an absolute statistical guarantee for any future orders. Long-term reliability will come from the repetition of the same consistent practices, not from a slogan.

Ultimately, success hinges on a few key factors: a Production environment, explicit families, leases closed once, small increments, two interchangeable forges, and no implicit transmission.

The system has become more reliable because it has finally agreed to become simpler once again.

Quick read

The day begins with a newcomer from the world of AI. Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 on 16 July: an open model with 2.8 trillion parameters using a mixture of experts, a context window of one million tokens, with full weights announced for 27 July. At 09:54, Kimi Code CLI is installed on the Mac with K3 as the default model. Claude Code launched the project, Codex has been running it since April; a third tool is now under observation.

The afternoon and evening are spent back in the workshop with one guiding principle: to close the doors that have been left ajar. Five pull requests tighten up the currency, configuration, sessions and emails, without touching the core of the editor.

Web PDFs are no longer free; they must be purchased

PR #321 is the centrepiece. The paid web PDF can no longer be enabled by the customer via the project’s options: entitlement is conditional upon a WooCommerce order that has actually been paid for.

The security hardening is methodical. An unknown order status is no longer treated as paid. Entitlement keys are frozen as soon as an order is linked, and the freeze decision is made under write protection. Rights already granted via authorised paths are preserved, including for refresh, rotation and GOF rendering, and legacy orders without a status remain accepted so as not to break existing functionality.

The GOF configuration belongs to the admin

PR #322 restricts GOF configuration to the ‘admin’ role. URLs are validated; the URL policy also applies to pairing; and the ‘Auto GOF’ toggle is hidden from the ‘editor’ role. A workshop editor no longer has access to the settings that determine production.

The details that matter

Three shorter fixes round off the day. PR #324 preserves the colours of shared clipart, which were being lost during public viewing. PR #325 secures reset logs and hard-codes the email webhook variables, with production secrets set in the test. PR #327 revokes the Better Auth session on logout, restricts the catch-all `auth-v2`, limits revocation to the current session and properly expires the ` __Secure-`-prefixed cookie in production.

A day of fine-tuning

Nothing spectacular on screen, but it’s the sort of day that makes the beta worth defending: the money follows the order, the configuration follows the role, the session follows the logout. And this morning, almost in passing, the workshop has undergone a transformation: a new Frontier open-weight model has arrived, and its CLI is already installed on the machine.

  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 786h11+ (779h00+ as at 20 July following historical correction, + 7h11+ observed)

Quick read

Following Tuesday’s break, Wednesday evening saw eight KEREDIT pull requests and two GOF pull requests consolidated in just under seven hours. The overarching principle: what the user sees when sharing or placing an order must be exactly what the production environment expects.

Meanwhile, this log is changing hands. The catch-up entries for days 117 to 119 are being written using Kimi Code CLI, installed on Monday morning: the first proper session using the tool on the repository, three days after the release of Kimi K3.

Never take an order at face value

PR #328 tightens up the WooCommerce pipeline. KEREDIT orders are re-verified via the Woo REST API before going into production, and an unreadable status is rejected rather than interpreted. The items in the re-validated order are also validated, and their role — main product or add-on — is compared with what the webhook had announced. The original order is no longer set in stone: it is re-validated at the moment it is processed by the workshop.

Public sharing becomes a real achievement

Three PRs follow one another on the public reader. #329 enables the GOF v2 web PDF to be downloaded from the share, with a trusted status reader injected into the Woo feed test and vulnerable dependencies fixed in the process. #330 removes the blank tab that used to open with the public link. #332 prevents opening the link from triggering a new GOF rendering: viewing a share should never resemble a command.

Two infrastructure safeguards

PR #333 rewrites the Google Photos OAuth callback: no more code injection into the redirect page, and a response compliant with the Content Security Policy. Logging into the client’s photo account remains seamless, but the redirect page can no longer be used as a script vector.

PR #335 blocks images larger than 100 megapixels from the asset pipeline: rejection occurs before decoding, goes through the standard business logic rejection, properly rejects catalogues that are too large at the upload confirmation stage, and the ` ASSET_PIPELINE_MAX_INPUT_PIXELS` limit has been extended all the way to the VPS composer, without duplication in the worker.

The evening wasn’t over yet

The first version of this post ended here, at 19:06. However, Git shows that the second half of the session was even more substantial than the first.

KEREDIT first learnt to regenerate an existing Production v2 without losing its product families. The bindings now follow an explicit rendering iteration; the web PDF download uses the current artefact, and WooCommerce replays recognise this new lineage. Polling remains read-only: checking the GOF status must never overwrite the production environment it is monitoring.

Templates are also locked on the server

At the same time, a long series of fixes has hardened the exact variants of templates. The format change preserves the proven geometry; permissions and visual identity are compared against a canonical baseline; cross-page movements are controlled; and late writes are locked out.

The key point is simple: a client may modify what the template permits, but must not silently reconstruct the contract from a more permissive payload.

GOF 0.8.0 makes iterations immutable

GOF begins the sequence at 0.7.3 with the Accurio auto-submission, bounded by a timestamped activation. Then PR #85 introduces 0.8.0 and the Production v2 rendering iterations.

A regeneration now creates an immutable candidate. The current PDF remains available until its atomic promotion; incidents and resubmissions remain linked to their iteration; and a previous iteration can no longer initiate an Accurio action. Rendering and delivery become two separate decisions, with a usable history rather than a current file being overwritten.

Kimi keeps the log

Last piece of news for today, and by no means the least important for this log: the documentation catch-up itself is carried out using Kimi Code CLI. The tool reads the repository, retrieves the evidence from Git, follows the blog skill procedure and produces posts 117, 118 and 119 in the usual format. Claude Code kicked off the venture, Codex has carried it this far; Kimi K3 is cutting its teeth on the project’s history, and it is this log that will remember it.

Correction of 4 August

This post was revised with Codex on 4 August 2026 following a comparison of the KEREDIT and GOF Git histories. The time window, versions, minimum time and cumulative total were recalculated to include the second half of the evening.

  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 794h07+ (786h11+ as of 22 July, + 7h56+ today)

Quick read

The night of 22nd to 23rd does not change the subject: it changes the scale. After stabilising the GOF iterations and regenerations, KEREDIT is closing, one by one, the remaining open doors around the product.

This isn’t a day of spectacular new features. It’s a day when the beta learns to say no: to reject a bypassed permission, an unsigned CSRF token, an unaccepted artefact, an overly permissive URL, a tenant leak or an unlimited upload.

Templates regain authority

The first commits finalise the previous day’s work on the template variants. Fine-grained permissions are resolved before the merge between variant and project, legacy flags are assigned explicit values, the exact variant is cleaned up before validation, and frozen shares progress atomically towards the correct rendering.

The server no longer relies solely on the client’s interpretation. The geometry, visual identity and permissions locks become a backend contract, which protects both the client editor and the builder.

The shared content follows the correct GOF iteration

Several PRs ensure the share is consistent with support regenerations. The public PDF follows the GOF job and the iteration actually rendered, accepts the latest web artefact still readable from a failed production run, requires an accepted PDF and retains a viewable version whilst a new one is being generated.

The expected result is simple: a sharing link must neither accidentally display an old file, nor cause a valid PDF to disappear because the subsequent production run encountered an incident.

Authentication and URLs become context-sensitive

The ‘Better Auth’ hardening ties CSRF to the session context, partitions tokens, enforces a twelve-character length for the relevant forms, and rejects unsigned tokens as soon as a session exists. At the same time, asset URLs validate their original target, serve SVGs as attachments, use a dedicated secret and calculate their TTL from the actual time of issue.

These are two versions of the same principle: a proof is only valid within its context, for a limited duration and for a specific purpose.

Workers must tell the truth

Catalogues and preview updates are aligned with the work actually being processed. An asset is no longer marked as ‘pending’ if no job exists, and a future thumbnail key is no longer persisted until the actual completion of processing. The back office therefore stops displaying promises that the worker cannot yet fulfil.

Closing the day by setting limits

The end of the session tightens public boundaries, staff access to tenant-scope, WooCommerce secrets, bearer authentication and the entropy of the GOF pairing code. Above all, it adds upload quotas, session rate limits and the purging of abandoned uploads.

Following this merge, Git shows no further KEREDIT or GOF activity until 30 July. Looking back on 4 August, this lull also reflects the passage of time, holidays and fatigue. The break is not a gap to be glossed over: it forms part of the project’s actual rhythm.

Quick read

The repository remained quiet from 24 to 29 July. On the 30th, the return did not take the form of a major new feature: it pieced things together, restored useful logs and put a clean release branch back onto the VPS.

It’s a busy day, at times thankless. It involves handling the workload, emails, dependencies, customer messages, the WordPress shop basket and the workshop revenue. Yet its guiding principle is clear: to pick up where we left off after the break without leaving multiple competing versions in the branches, releases or tools.

Recovering what might otherwise have been left behind

Two rescue branches preserve an editor load campaign and a snapshot prior to the IPTC project. The ‘dev’ branch then recovers a realistic editor session scenario, the log for Days 117 to 119, and the map of recent releases.

This consolidation is not merely a Git tidy-up. It prevents load tests, editorial decisions or fixes that have already been reviewed from becoming trapped in a forgotten branch upon returning from holiday.

Email and dependencies are included in the contract

The WordPress connector gains an authenticated REST endpoint to send KEREDIT reset emails. The release metadata and the manifest checksum have been aligned. At the same time, four vulnerabilities high in the CI audit gate have been fixed, and historical transitive dependencies have been refreshed without breaking the toolchains still in use.

The objective is less visible than a new screen, but essential for the beta: the user must receive their email, and the pipeline that produces it must remain deployable without any known security vulnerabilities.

Explaining quotas instead of speaking like a server

Upload quota errors are rewritten for the end user: the cause and possible action are stated simply, without infrastructure jargon. The local composer also publishes services on the IPv4 and IPv6 loopbacks so that localhost does not become unpredictable depending on the machine.

The package thus combines two forms of reliability: an error must be understood by the client, and the same local environment must respond consistently on Macs as well as on previous machines.

Resuming a project without introducing unintended changes

The shopping basket recovery feature corrects an unintended version update. Opening a project should no longer trigger an autosave, a new version or a re-validation by the sales team if the price, format, quantity and options remain unchanged. The connector also correctly encodes empty dictionaries for simple products, and release archives become reproducible.

The customer’s action once again matches what they intend to do: resume and view, not silently modify the basket.

The acceptance test must never deliver to Accurio

Since GOF 0.8.0, the Accurio handover has been separated from the rendering. KEREDIT has therefore removed the old contract capture from its v2 acceptance test and now proves the absence of a live handover instead of waiting for a pseudo-verdict of ‘not sent’. Automated validation can test the entire workflow without requiring a delivery client or risking an actual transmission.

The release is finalised on KEREDIT 0.16.16; check on the VPS that the SHA merges. After a turbulent week, this is the right way to resume: fewer promises, a single line dev, and a verifiable source.

The work is brief and structural. The dashboard must no longer deduce the status of the P340 and i5 machines from the old global snapshot. Production v2 already has its own tables, retries, leases and heartbeats; the interface must read this data directly.

The v2 registry becomes nominal

Measuring activity, not adding noise

Historical durations are grouped by activity windows. The dashboard can thus compare machines without repeatedly adding up fragments that belong to the same job. It is a minor model adjustment, but it determines future decisions regarding capacity and switching between forges.

GOF is moving to ‘0.8.1’ with this clarified source of truth.

A CI that doesn’t get blocked by its cache

PR #89 rounds off the session by making the inline publication cache non-blocking. A cache should speed up a build; it should never become a new reason not to publish the forge.

After three days without a commit, this brief resumption does not seek to make up for lost time. It simply puts observability back where it belongs: on the persistent facts of Production v2.

The day begins with measurement and ends with tidying up. KEREDIT now has a more realistic load campaign, the transitive vulnerabilities in the CI gate have been resolved, and the security audit has become a scheduled task on the repository runner.

Then the work turns to its own history. The log had not progressed since 22 July. Time, the holidays and fatigue had led one to believe there was a massive backlog; the records reveal a gentler reality: nine calendar days without a commit, a few very busy days, and above all, posts that could still be reconstructed without having to make things up.

A release that feels more like a beta

PR #369 reworks the editor session scenario around the current login, explicit thresholds and a selective payload manifest. The campaign reaches 50 virtual users with a reproducible report, without loading all image sets in every scenario.

This work does not guarantee that the beta will handle every peak. It provides a replayable baseline, observable thresholds and a common vocabulary for comparing the next campaign with this one.

Security must be addressed every week

PR #370 aligns fast-uri and brace-expansion with the versions addressing the security advisories tracked by the repository. PR #371 adds a weekly audit and standardises the use of the Mac runner keredit-ci as a known service on the workstation.

The key change is the frequency. A one-off audit indicates that the repository was clean on a given day; a scheduled audit allows us to see when it ceases to be so.

Cleaning up without erasing history

Local tidying removes old GOF checkouts, archives a NAS context file and sends unwanted artefacts to the Bin. Version history retains the list, the justifications and the items deliberately kept.

The same principle applies to the log: we can remove noise without deleting the history. The entry from 24 June is restored, the one from 22 July is complete, and those from 23 July, 30 July and 3 August are returned to their correct places.

Time is recalculated

The previous cumulative total of 740h19+ was too low. It omitted 24 minutes on 1 May, six hours on 24 June, and four days from 25 to 28 June, which were left out of the calculation. The update adds 41h05+ even before the end of July, then reinstates the long evening of 22 July, the sessions on 23 and 30 July and the one on 3 August.

This total remains a minimum. It does not convert breaks into working time and does not claim to measure CI expectations, conversations, manual tests or fatigue exactly. It simply brings the tally back into line with what the records still allow us to prove.

body.text:
Session timetables

  • Agent used: Kimi CLI code for Woo synchronisation, Codex running in parallel on the Products & Prices workspace
  • Main environment: Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz, VPS [nom privé], server [nom privé] (ooblik.com)
  • Date covered: Wednesday 5 August 2026
  • Main branch prior to the log: dev, PRs #387 to #393 merged
  • Observed windows: approximately 16:30 → 19:45 CEST for end-to-end Woo synchronisation
  • Minimum observed duration: approximately 3 hours+
  • Main releases: Products & Prices workspace 0.17.0, automatic product synchronisation KEREDIT → WooCommerce, plugin 0.1.89, deployment 0.17.1
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 807h37+ (804h37+ as at 4 August, + 3h00+ today)

Quick read

The day began with a minor scare: a product listing edited in KEREDIT wasn’t displaying correctly on the WooCommerce side. Immediate frustration. Then it all came back to me: the WooCommerce listing had never been resynchronised — I needed to open the product in WooCommerce and click ‘Synchronise’. The bug wasn’t in the code, it was in the action.

Rather than getting used to the process, the day puts an end to it. In the evening, a backup in the KEREDIT admin panel updates the WooCommerce listing all by itself, in just a few seconds, as demonstrated on ooblik.com.

Diagnosis before the code

The investigation first confirms what’s already in place: the synchronisation is a ‘pull’ operation; the WordPress plugin retrieves the product configuration via the KEREDIT API. Two automatic triggers already exist — the save of the Woo listing and a lazy refresh on display, limited to one hour. The gap is clear: editing the listing in the KEREDIT admin panel doesn’t notify anyone.

Three options are on the table: a real-time webhook push, a simply hardened pull, or a WordPress price list cron job. The choice falls on the push, because the scenario we’re dealing with is exactly ‘I’ve just made a change, I’ll test it straight away’.

The decisions that matter

First decision: no Prisma migration for the secret. The backend only stores the hash of the integration secret, so it can never send it back to the plugin. The environment variables WOO_SITE_URL, WOO_INTEGRATION_KEY and WOO_INTEGRATION_SECRET follow the precedent AUTH_EMAIL_WEBHOOK_* — duplication assumed, single-tenant architecture required.

Second decision: the notification is ‘fire-and-forget’. Five-second timeout, error logged as a ‘warn’, failures are never escalated to the admin dashboard. An unreachable WooCommerce site must not cause a product page to fail.

Third decision: on the plugin side, the HTTP response is sent immediately and the actual synchronisation is scheduled via wp_schedule_single_event. The backend does not wait for WordPress.

The usual stress of ‘doing things properly’

The configuration requires production credentials. These are stored in the plugin settings on the ooblik.com server. WP-CLI with PHP 8.3 explicitly — the default binary points to a PHP version that’s too old and misrepresents the versions — allows you to read them properly, to enter the local .env and that of the VPS, and to validate the Compose output before any restart. The backend is not restarted straight away: the old code is still running, so the variables will have to wait until deployment.

Deployment follows its own procedure: version 0.17.0 is already live, so we need a 0.17.1, which means a release branch, a PR, a successful CI run, and a merge. Then the nominal script runs, the served SHA is verified, and only after that does the test run.

Proof, twice

The first end-to-end test fails — the meta _keredit_connector_synced_at doesn’t change. A few seconds of doubt, then the obvious realisation: the test backup ran during redeployment, on the old code. The channel is manually verified from within the container (200, scheduled: true), the user re-registers, and the meta updates automatically. Second time lucky.

The ‘Synchronise’ button remains visible in WooCommerce. It’s no longer needed, but you don’t remove an emergency ramp on the day you install the lift.

body.text:
Session timetables

  • Agent used: Kimi CLI code for catalogue synchronisation, Codex running in parallel for basket discounts
  • Main environment: Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz, VPS [nom privé], server [nom privé] (ooblik.com)
  • Date covered: Thursday 6 August 2026, from the night of 5 to 6 until the end-of-day handover
  • Main branch prior to the log: dev, PRs #394 to #413 merged or committed during the day
  • Time slots selected for the minimum: approximately 00:15 → 03:30, 11:13 → 11:34 and 15:35 → 22:58 CEST; commits continued until 04:19, without including CI waiting time and deployment verification in the total
  • Minimum time observed: approximately 10 hours 59 minutes+
  • Main batches: real-time catalogue synchronisation and hardening, basket discounts up to the rule by different products (0.20.0), persistent deletion (0.19.3), resilient basket validation (0.19.4), scoping followed by implementation of the dynamic product preview
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 818h36+ (807h37+ as at 5 August, + 10h59+ today)

Quick read

Yesterday, the ‘Synchronise’ button was removed for product records. This night, the change has been extended to cover everything else: papers, workshop and library attributes, pricing matrices, MISKISS recipes, and the creation and deletion of products. The target is: a few seconds between a change in KEREDIT and its reflection on ooblik.com.

Meanwhile, another session is delivering basket discounts on WooCommerce — a feature that was anticipated, accepted, then reworked that very same night when the actual business rule (‘per visual’, not ‘per cumulative items’) replaced the first version. Two developers, a single repository, a single production environment: it’s going to be a long night.

The gap in coverage

The question that sets everything in motion is an innocent one: “If I rename a product in KEREDIT, do I need to do anything to see the change on WooCommerce?” Honest answer: no. The notification was only triggered when the product record was saved; shared repositories followed different paths. A paper renaming would only have been visible after the one-hour TTL had elapsed.

The chosen design: a catalogue-side plugin version. For targeted changes, we resynchronise the product; for changes to shared data sources, we invalidate everything and resynchronise in the background, triggered immediately by spawn_cron() without waiting for site traffic. On the backend, a three-second debounce prevents bursts of updates from triggering bursts of notifications.

The midnight collision

Plugin 0.1.90 is built, tested and ready for release. And then, the unthinkable: dev has changed during implementation. The ‘reset basket’ session has merged, bumping the application to 0.18.0 — and it has itself published a 0.1.90 plugin, without the synchronisation code. Same version number, two different sets of content. Publishing over the top would render any site that’s already up to date unusable: WordPress never offers the same version twice.

Decision made in thirty seconds: renumber. The catalogue synchronisation becomes 0.1.91, the changelog clearly distinguishes between the two batches, and the manifest is rebuilt with the actual checksum. The following night confirmed that this instinct was the right one: the version number of a published artefact is never reused.

The rebase, however, went badly the first time round — conflicts, stash, the scare of a ` reset --hard` on uncommitted user files, recovered just in time from a stash that had become dangling. A lesson learnt once again: when two sessions are working on the same worktree, stash early, stash often.

Deadlines don’t sleep

The deployment safeguard then rejects 0.18.1 until the version moves forward: unsurprisingly, 0.18.0 has just been deployed by the other session. Release branch, PR, CI, merge — the ritual, all over again. Then the 0.1.91 plugin is published and installed, the backend deployed, and the long-awaited test arrives at 2.03 am: renaming a document in KEREDIT. Four seconds later, _keredit_connector_synced_at is up and running on ooblik.com. The coverage is complete, the proof is in, the coffee’s cold.

The night isn’t over yet. Two minor issues are sorted out straight away: catalog-changed was returning a 400 instead of a 401 without credentials — WordPress validates route parameters before permission, a documented pitfall, and is locked down by a test — and the pricing matrices, such as the MISKISS are now included in the synchronisation scope. A new version numbering conflict arose in the process, as version 0.19.0 of the visual discounts was released ahead of the planned 0.18.2: the changelog entry was renumbered as 0.19.1, moved to the the top, and it is this version that goes into production that very night (the log is closed before the deployment is actually complete, subsequently verified: SHA served and container intact).

Opinion piece: are two agents better than one?

Night-time productivity is very real: three application versions, three plugin versions, ten merged PRs, two features delivered and tested in production. The hidden cost is just as real: version conflicts, rebases, contradictory manifests, and that particular kind of exhaustion that comes from having to re-read a changelog conflict at 3 am, wondering which session is correct.

The rule that emerges is not to slow down, but to make conflicts painless: version numbers that are never reused, small and frequent releases, deployment safeguards that reject rather than guess, and a single place — the changelog — to document afterwards who did what. The ‘Synchronise’ button, meanwhile, is permanently dormant.

The day after the night

The first post was written and merged at 3.11 am. It faithfully recounted the night, but not yet the day that was to follow. The recovery began with a very specific bug: deleting a discount slot only deleted its local draft. Upon reloading, the slot reappeared. The ‘Trash’ action has therefore become a truly persistent operation, with the draft restored in the event of failure and the card locked whilst the save is in progress. The convention is then documented: in a self-saving card, a destructive action cannot simply modify the React state.

The WooCommerce basket receives the same reliability treatment. Brief backend outages during redeployment should no longer alarm the customer with a permanent error. The plugin retries transient errors within a limited quota, retains an identical validation for two minutes, but always revalidates at checkout. The Codex review has tightened the quota and safeguards: an arbitrary integration header must not allow the limit to be circumvented, and wc-ajax=checkout must follow exactly the same contract.

The discount has reverted to its standard business rule

Last night’s functionality was still too complex. Following acceptance testing, the model has been simplified: a product family includes different products, regardless of the quantities printed. The volume discount on print runs remains part of the product price; the basket discount remains a family-level rule. This change removes more code than it adds and results in version 0.20.0.

At the same time, catalogue synchronisation has been made more robust: no notification when an import is rejected, a new run when a change occurs during resynchronisation, and more cautious finalisation of the pipeline. These changes will not be fully finalised until the following early morning, following the review feedback and the release of version 0.20.1.

The product is starting to take shape

The end of the day finally sees work begin on the visible aspect: separating the print-ready composition from the commercial presentation. A decision tree sets the course, then the implementation adds colours, textures and conditional designs that can be controlled via product options. These layers appear on the canvas and in the thumbnails, but remain out of thepages_datas and PDFs. This is a significant product milestone: KEREDIT can display a spiral, an elastic band or a cover without asking GOF to print them.

The day ends with an external incident: GitHub Actions needs to be restarted following an outage. The work is in place, but its merge and release are scheduled for 7 August. The initial commit was therefore just in time for the night; this catch-up gives it the second session it was missing.
