body.text:
Session timetables

  • Tool used: Codex, with several automated work sessions and reviews
  • Primary environment: Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz, GitHub Actions and KEREDIT VPS for the relevant releases
  • Date covered: Friday 7 August 2026, including the night shift starting on 6 August
  • Main branch: dev, PRs #412, #414 to #417 and #425 to #427 merged; Builder work continued at the end of the session
  • Observed windows: 03:06 → 04:33 and 17:07 → 22:12 CEST
  • Minimum observed duration: approximately 6h32+
  • Milestone commits: ba8245c4, 73b66942, 01dfe415, 2d942516, 663636b1, 54b1a54e, 5a3e853c
  • Versions used: 0.20.1, 0.21.0, 0.21.1 and 0.21.2; plugin 0.1.96 then 0.1.97
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 825h08+ (818h36+ as at 6 August, + 6h32+ today)

Quick read

The day begins by tidying up the loose ends from the previous day: the WooCommerce synchronisation is now recoverable, compatible with the old endpoint and capable of handling a change received whilst a batch is running. Then KEREDIT changes gear. The product can finally feature a dynamic presentation without cluttering its print file; the basket protects the projects it references; the pricing grid accepts a free value for each format × quantity combination; the Builder is starting to become the sole authoring tool for templates.

These are not four isolated functions. They are beginning to form a single contract: a marketable product links a composition, an appearance, a price and a project without confusing their sources of truth.

Finishing the Woo synchronisation properly

The night-time session processes Codex feedback from catalogue synchronisation. The backend falls back to /product-synced when a site is still using an older plugin. The plugin maintains its lock throughout the processing of batches, then symmetrically re-checks the pending generation before exiting. A merged burst must not lose either legacy products or the latest update received.

The security fix js-yaml is included in the same release. Version 0.20.1 and plugin 0.1.96 are prepared, documented and then merged at 4.33 am, following the return of GitHub Actions. The night finally draws to a close with a publishable state rather than just a successful restart.

Showcasing the product without rendering its background

The dynamic product preview, introduced the day before, is merged into 0.21.0. The references in the workshop library can provide a colour or a physical texture; the Builder links these appearances to a family of options and adds conditional backgrounds. Layers follow the layout in the canvas, page thumbnails and project previews.

The key principle can be summed up in one sentence: the presentation is not the composition. It remains separate from the print JSON and the PDF. A single template can therefore be used for several products or colourways without duplicating its pages, whilst the appearance assets remain protected as long as they are referenced.

A project viewed in the basket is no longer disposable

The second major benefit stems from a more subtle risk. A WooCommerce line item may still point to a project that the client subsequently deletes in KEREDIT. ` cart_seen_at` becomes the minimal record of the project’s passage through the basket: for 90 rolling days, all deletion interfaces — client, application and admin, whether individual or batch — refuse to delete this project. Revenue projects test_flux remain unaffected, but only via their persistent and tenant-scoped identity.

Plugin 0.1.97 can also account for an old line that has already become orphaned. The guard does not repair the pass; above all, it prevents it from being reproduced.

The price becomes an explicit matrix

The historical additive mode can start from a base price and apply tiered pricing or surcharges. It cannot simply express that each format × quantity combination has its own price. The product listing therefore gains a matrix_v1 grid, embedded in the Product.pricing contract, validated before saving and utilised by the server, the editor and WooCommerce.

Review has revealed a legacy issue: the VAT rate has existed in several different formats. The runtime standardises the old values and guarantees a default rate; otherwise, the basket discount would be calculated on an inconsistent basis. Version 0.21.2 brings together the matrix, its VAT compatibility and the Builder’s first atomic guarantees.

The Builder becomes the control centre

Multi-format saving can no longer promote one variant whilst others are still being written. Ambiguous normalisations and migrations are detected, variants are compared semantically, pages are realigned after saving, and promotion remains locked until the operation is complete. This first batch corresponds to issue #418 and closes the main atomicity flaw.

Late in the evening, the next task begins: removing the templates list’s role as a concurrent editor and centralising the reference product, assignments, publication and transfers within the Builder. The commit 5a3e853c establishes this new control centre, but its PR and final patches will be merged after midnight. Day 126 therefore ends with a clear boundary and work still in progress, not at a false finish line.

Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex, with multiple sessions, automatic reviews and related work in GOF
  • Main environment: Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz, GOF repository dépôt local gof, GitHub Actions
  • Date covered: Saturday 8 August 2026, following on directly from the evening of the 7th
  • Main branches and PRs: dev, feat/421-composition-produit, feat/422-client-permissions, feat/423-layouts-composition-import, test/424-builder-library-client-pdf, codex/fix-print-quantity-contract; PRs #428, #429, #430, #431, #432, #434 to #440 and #442 merged

  • Minimum duration observed: approximately 12h42+
  • Versions affected: 0.21.3, 0.21.4, 0.22.0, 0.22.1 and 0.22.2
  • Key traces: 71 non-synthetic Git commits identified in KEREDIT, thirteen PRs merged during the day, GOF commit 211f926
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 837h50+ (825h08+ as at 7 August, + 12h42+ today)

Quick read

The work started yesterday in the Template Builder is becoming an almost complete workflow. KEREDIT can simulate a product, distinguish between what will be printed and what is used to present it, manage the customisation options available to the customer, import layouts without distorting them, and then go through the entire workflow right up to the PDF v2. The end of the day brings us back to the business side and clears up another ambiguity: for photo and fine art prints, the quantity sold is the actual number of images, not a value derived from a description or the number of pages.

At GOF, another question arises in the middle of the night: how to demonstrate a future multi-tenant SaaS solution without rewriting the code base or confusing proof with a product promise. The scope remains documentary and limited. It does not alter the current workshop priority.

A Builder that finally lets you try things out

The simulation bench and the ‘Test as the customer’ mode give the Builder a direct verification loop. The test is ephemeral: it alters neither the source document nor its history. Specialised surfaces remain locked when they need to be, the geometry of the coverings is simulated, and the variants already saved no longer disappear in the process.

This simulation also makes it necessary to distinguish between two concepts that were previously too closely linked. ‘Printed composition’ shows the document that will go to production; ‘assembled product’ adds the colours, textures and designs needed to understand the item being sold. The canvas, the page rail and the overall view follow the same convention. The commercial design remains outside the PDF.

Allowing flexibility without losing the template

Client permissions are no longer a pile of implicit exceptions. Explicit profiles and local decisions — inherit, allow, disallow — are handled in the same way by both the frontend and the backend. The composition import preserves these freedoms, the layouts and the elements that the user must still be able to modify.

The pricing grid receives two visible adjustments in parallel: it becomes a proper bordered table, then balances its columns and makes it clear whether a cell represents the total including VAT for the batch or the unit price. When this format × quantity matrix is activated, the effects of the two axes are no longer added a second time to the quotation.

The vertical layout replaces the intuitive approach

The largest batch adds almost no visible functionality. It demonstrates that the Workshop Library, the multi-format Builder, the simulation, the disposable client test, a real client project, the catalogue and publication can all remain consistent within the same workflow. The workflow extends right down to the actual PDF v2 queues and workers.

Two PDF artefacts are observed. The tests also prove the absence of any leakage: neither the product appearance nor the Accurio delivery note must appear in the print-ready document. This boundary is more important than simply the green colour of the corporate identity, as it verifies the terms of the KEREDIT → GOF contract.

Print runs are restored to their actual quantities

The evening session finalises the review feedback on print quantities. The products photo_print and fine_art_print are not paginated products. Their minimum, maximum and pitch settings become authoritative in quantity_rule, and the quantity ordered corresponds to the actual total number of photos or artworks.

The migration of old settings remains unchanged in Prisma, but several fixes are required to limit legacy processing, retain the auto-save function when a price is rejected, and ensure that quotes, shopping baskets and orders all use the same total. Two successive PRs complete the batch: the first delivers the contract, the second addresses the discrepancies found during review.

GOF monitors the SaaS without leaving the workshop

The external repository dépôt local gof receives the commit 211f926. It adds a roadmap, a test PRD and six decisions: explicit organisation and site structure, TenantContext, PostgreSQL and storage isolation, an outbound Accurio connector, modularisation of the table, and a usage ledger separate from invoicing.

The approach remains cautious: retaining the forge, proving isolation with two organisations, and not turning a test into a commercial re-design. KEREDIT remains the authority for orders, projects and assets; GOF remains the consumer of a versioned payload. Today’s post may seem massive because it is: a lot is changing, but the overarching aim is primarily to better separate responsibilities.

The start of a worktree discipline

A second milestone belongs to this day, even though the commit wouldn’t happen until six days later. The worktree krampouz-worktree-workflow was created at 09:32 and the first workflow files were modified that morning. The aim is simple: to ensure that two Codex sessions no longer share a branch, a worktree or a release number by accident.

The future ‘worktree-chantier’ skill formalises a dedicated branch, an isolated directory, the explicit copying of the environment only when necessary, and a clean-up process that does not destroy anything until the work is published or preserved. At the same time, the deployment workflow learns to verify its starting point.

This discipline stems directly from the issues encountered in previous days. It does not deliver any client functionality, but seeks to reduce the human cost of parallel sessions. However, the work remains open and uncommitted at the end of the day: even a sound procedure can become an afterthought if its completion is postponed.

body.text:
Session timetables

  • Tool used: Codex, with the Impeccable review and hardening workflow for the publisher
  • Primary environment: Mac, multiple KEREDIT worktrees, GitHub Actions and supplier search
  • Date covered: Tuesday 18 August 2026
  • Main branches: codex/impeccable-editor-hardening merged into dev via PR #443; storage audit retained uncommitted in codex/vrifier-ltat-de-la-branche
  • Time window used for the minimum: 17:44 → 19:00 CEST, from the creation of the storage analysis to the worktree snapshot
  • Minimum time observed: approximately 1h16+
  • Released version: 0.22.4, merge PR #443 f2b46361
  • Key milestones: storage analysis created at 17:44, seven hardening commits, green CI and journey, final Codex review with no major issues, snapshot a276f248
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 842h53+ (841h37+ as at 15 August, plus 1h16+ today)

Quick read

Two forms of validation are being worked on in the same window. In the editor, KEREDIT must be certain that a project has been saved before allowing the user to exit or submit. In the infrastructure, a desire to leave Cloudflare R2 must not result in a migration to the first European provider that comes along.

The first set of features is delivered in 0.22.4. The second remains a local analysis, not yet committed. Yet both apply the same rule: do not confuse a reassuring interface with a proven guarantee.

The backup becomes a barrier

The publisher now blocks both exit and command operations until a strict backup has been confirmed. Version conflicts remain distinct from transient errors: the former require a decision, whilst the latter must be able to be queued and retried.

The checkout explains more clearly why it is unavailable. The save statuses, keyboard controls and ARIA states are aligned. At medium width, the editor, the Template Builder and its client-side test no longer leave two side panels competing for space; the wide layout retains its behaviour.

PR #443 was short in duration but yielded a wealth of feedback. Several reviews were requested on successive HEADs to correct the CI security checks, responsive coverage, panel consistency and the requeueing of autosave. The CI and the ‘journey’ workflow are approved, and the final review finds no further major issues. The merge takes place at 6.47 pm.

Exiting R2 without triggering another outage

The storage audit begins with an encouraging finding: KEREDIT is already largely S3-compatible. Objects are referenced by key, URLs are signed on the fly and the backend hides the provider. The migration can therefore be a simple switchover of configuration and data.

However, the research rules out Hetzner as a viable option. The Object Storage service is experiencing a prolonged capacity degradation, with no SLA suited to a synchronous upload flow. OVH 1-AZ and Scaleway have also experienced recent incidents. The analysis identifies OVH Standard 3-AZ Paris as the leading candidate and IONOS Frankfurt as an alternative to test, but no migration decision has yet been implemented.

The real takeaway of the day is not a provider’s logo. It is the need for retries with backoff, proper tracking of 5xx errors and a copy with a second provider. Changing buckets without these safeguards would merely shift the vulnerability.

The pace is faltering

The log has already been interrupted for ten days. Yet the code continues to progress in dense batches, with repeated reviews and a new infrastructure decision to be made. The contrast is becoming difficult to bear: the technical evidence is piling up, but the sense of progress is no longer keeping pace. This day does not yet bear the most candid words on exhaustion; it reveals the conditions leading to it.

title.text: Day 130 – Save before you exit, choose before you migrate

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Browser used: Codex
  • Primary environment: Mac, KEREDIT repository dépôt local krampouz, OVH and IONOS consoles, local S3 POC
  • Date covered: Thursday 20 August 2026; full report to follow after the session ends
  • Branches observed: codex/vrifier-ltat-de-la-branche then the branch from PR #444 merged into dev
  • Time window selected for the minimum: 16:08 → 19:12 CEST, from initial work on the POC to the final commit of the GOF audit
  • Minimum time observed: approximately 3 hours 4 minutes+, excluding research, supplier trials and conversations that cannot be reconstructed with a time stamp
  • Version delivered: 0.22.5, merge PR #444 d1a3acee
  • Main result: OVH Standard 3-AZ Paris validated via POC and benchmark from the VPS; IONOS abandoned; no migration carried out yet
  • Key logs: storage health admin page, R2/OVH benchmark, release 0.22.5 and audit of the GOF integration up to 3db0ed44
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 845h57+ (842h53+ as at 18 August, plus 3h04+ today)

Quick read

The storage POC provides a viable solution. OVH Standard 3-AZ Paris accepts the current KEREDIT stream: CORS, pre-signed PUTs with and without checksums, multipart, signed GETs and cleaning operations all pass. IONOS has been ruled out prior to technical testing due to issues with its onboarding process, a poor interface and an SLA that is too weak to make the effort economically viable.

Another infrastructure option, Forgejo, has been explicitly classified as zero priority. GitHub remains the source of truth and nothing should be migrated in advance. These two decisions narrow the technical scope. They do not automatically reduce the workload.

Sovereignty becomes a concrete architecture

The choice is not merely about a faster storage bucket. KEREDIT handles photos, projects and production documents belonging to OOBLIK’s clients. The aim is therefore to keep their data journey within Europe: the in Germany, object storage with OVH in France, in the Paris 3-AZ region. Moving away from R2, a service provided by an American company, removes the primary storage from the scope of the Cloud Act and makes the location more transparent.

This sovereignty is not presented as absolute. Cloudflare services may still be used outside the storage environment, and a European architecture does not exempt organisations from the need for backups, encryption or access control. The benefit of the day is more specific: client objects now have a French target that is proven to be compatible, whilst the application remains hosted in Germany.

The POC opts for OVH, with one caveat

The backend/scripts/poc-object-storage.mjs framework performs the functions on which KEREDIT actually depends. On OVH 3-AZ Paris, the bucket responds, the CORS rule is applied, the browser preflight is correct, simple and multipart uploads are successful, and signed GET URLs work. From the local workstation, the small GET request has a median time of around 32 ms and the 1 MB PUT takes around 570 ms. The measurement will need to be repeated from the VPS.

The SHA-256 checksum is accepted in the signature but is not validated by OVH: a deliberately corrupted body still receives a 200 response. This is not a blocking issue for the current workflow, which already places the checksum in the URL and confirms the upload on the backend side, but integrity then relies on TLS and this application-level validation. The log retains this caveat rather than turning a green POC into absolute certainty.

The benchmark is then run again from the production VPS. Compared to R2, OVH is approximately 2.6 times faster on the median for the 4 MB pre-signed PUT, 5.5 times faster for the small signed GET and 1.6 times faster for the 1 MB SDK PUT. Data sovereignty therefore does not require sacrificing performance in this case; the more variable p95 of the large PUT requests remains to be monitored.

The bucket and test keys must be revoked, as the credentials have been transmitted over an unsecured channel. No R2 copies, no switchover and no creation of production resources are initiated in this post.

Close the doors that do not lead to September

Forgejo is technically feasible, but it would affect repositories, issues, PRs, CI, GHCR, procedures gh and the Codex review. Now is not the right time. The ops documentation therefore sets out a decision not to take action: GitHub remains in place and any future evaluation will begin with an empty, isolated and reversible instance.

The storage migration itself is not yet a priority over the product. The useful outcome is a prepared plan and a roadmap: measure the actual volume, strengthen retry mechanisms and monitoring, and only then plan for mirroring, failover and rollback.

Rant: finally writing about burnout

The delay in posting this journal entry isn’t just a routine oversight. As the early September release approaches, the accumulated fatigue has become overwhelming: severe demotivation, doubts about my ability to meet the deadline and a feeling of being on the verge of burnout. I’m going through what feels like a mild depression, probably fuelled by exhaustion. Even tangible progress is no longer always enough to restore my drive.

I want to write about this honestly, because this state of mind is directly affecting the project: difficulty in wrapping up the day, temporarily giving up on the journal, decisions that feel more burdensome, and the impression that the release is drawing closer faster than the product is progressing. This post is not intended to dramatise the situation or to conclude that everything is going badly. It simply records a moment when continuing at the same pace is probably no longer sustainable.

I’m not going through this alone, though. I’ve had a rest, and Claire, my wife, is supporting me with her love. Her presence doesn’t take the fatigue away, but it changes the way I cope with it. In my own words today: ‘with love, everything passes’. This is also part of the truth of this period, and it deserves to be recorded in the journal just as much as the doubts.

The code repository tells a paradoxical story. Since the last post, the Builder has gone through the entire build chain, the print quantities have been made more reliable, the checkout process has been hardened and the storage option has been tested. So it is not the lack of results that is fuelling the doubt. It is the accumulation of issues, the approach of September and the gradual disappearance of any leeway to catch up.

The next milestone isn’t a new feature

The point is not to promise yet another sprint. We must first make the release clear: what is essential for early September, what is already sufficiently reliable, and what can wait. The log resumes today precisely for this reason. It is not just for counting commits; it must also prevent the project from overshadowing the person driving it.

title.text: Day 131 – The release is drawing near, my body’s saying ‘enough’

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: Mac, multiple KEREDIT worktrees, GitHub Actions and Hetzner VPS in Germany
  • Date covered: Friday 21 August 2026
  • Main branches: feat/presigned-upload-retry, codex/vrifier-ltat-de-la-branche and workflow branches, all merged into dev
  • Time window selected for the minimum: 11:05 – 12:46 CEST
  • Minimum duration observed: approximately 1h41+
  • Version released: 0.22.6, release 20f0f8c3
  • Main traces: 22 non-merge commits, PRs #445 to #447, upload retry and hardening of development workflows
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 847h38+ (845h57+ as at 20 August, plus 1h41+ today)

Quick read

The decision to use OVH has been made, but a preference for sovereignty is not enough to secure customers’ photos. Before switching providers, KEREDIT is hardening the most exposed operation: direct uploads from the browser to object storage. Pre-signed uploads now include a retry mechanism with exponential backoff, and the mobile flow has been integrated into the same sharing module as the rest of the frontend.

This step is less spectacular than copying a bucket. Yet it is essential to ensure that the switch from a US provider to a French storage service does not turn a laudable ambition into a step backwards for customers.

A European architecture must also keep outages brief

The future path is becoming clear: the application runs on the Hetzner VPS in Germany and client objects must reside with OVH in France. This European setup reduces the main storage’s exposure to the Cloud Act, but it does not eliminate network errors, 429 errors or 5xx errors from a provider.

The helper presignedUpload.ts therefore handles transient errors with an increasing wait time. The Codex review adjusts the backoff exponent, then verifies that the mobile path correctly uses this shared contract. The change is covered by unit tests and documented in BIBLIOTHEQUE.md.

Making the method as reliable as the product

The second part of the session focuses on Codex workflows and contextual documentation. Audits are now better at detecting skill snapshots, old directories that have been removed and renamed paths. Detached worktrees are verified against their actual base, and managed copies can no longer be overwritten silently.

This work may seem tangential to storage. Yet it serves the same purpose: a production switchover between KEREDIT and GOF requires knowing exactly which branch, which version and which procedure is currently in effect.

End-of-day status

KEREDIT 0.22.6 is delivered with the upload retry feature. No production objects have yet changed provider. The target remains OVH Standard 3-AZ Paris, R2 remains the active source, and the next step must be a reversible, measured and shared copy for both KEREDIT and GOF.

title.text: Day 133 – Customer data is on its way to Paris

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Agent used: Codex
  • Primary environment: Mac, KEREDIT production on a Hetzner VPS in Germany, OVH 3-AZ Paris, P340/i5 build servers and GOF repository dépôt local gof
  • Date covered: Sunday 23 August 2026
  • Main branches: feat/gof-admission-test-flux-flag, fix/e2e-journey-test-flux-echo, fix/test-flux-live-recovery-guard (KEREDIT branch); GOF PRs #90 and #91
  • Time window selected for the minimum: 09:59 – 16:33 CEST, KEREDIT and GOF tracks crossed
  • Minimum duration observed: approximately 6h34+
  • Version delivered: 0.22.8, release 9855526e; GOF aligned with 9c324f9
  • Main traces: PR KEREDIT #451 to #454, PR GOF #90/#91, green production acceptance and post-switchover campaign k6
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 866h13+ (859h39+ as at 22 August, + 6h34+ today)

Quick summary

The switchover is now effective and verifiable. KEREDIT now writes to krampouz-assets-prod at OVH 3-AZ Paris, GOF reads the assets and writes its artifacts to them, and the forges continue to receive only pre-signed ephemeral URLs. Customer data is stored in France; the core application remains on the European VPS in Germany.

This sovereignty-focused choice goes live with two pieces of evidence: no Accurio handover is triggered by the acceptance test, and performance is not compromised.

Resolving the risk identified the previous day

The ‘test_flux’ marker now passes through KEREDIT and GOF all the way to the persistent production environment. Readmissions where the marker diverges are refused. The KEREDIT acceptance test fails early if it encounters an unmarked live production environment and requires the marker to be echoed upon admission.

The final proof is deliberately robust: Auto Accurio remains active, the acceptance Production is marked test_flux, delivery equals none, transmitted remains false and no Accurio delivery lines are created. The complete PDF workflow is therefore executed on OVH without any risk of delivering a test job to the print shop.

Measure from Europe, don’t just take the provider’s word for it

The raw benchmark is run again from the VPS and from the production workstation. From the VPS, OVH is approximately 3.2 times faster than R2 on the pre-signed PUT of 4 Mio, 4 times faster on the signed GET and 3.4 times faster on the SDK PUT. From the workshop, the performance gains observed remain between 2.3 and 2.5 times.

The k6 campaign confirms the application’s behaviour: 1,693 complete iterations and 127,440 checks completed without failure on the editor-beta scenario at 50 VUs. The variants served by the proxy are 2 to 2.6 times faster, whilst the batch upload remains on a par because it is primarily dominated by the worker.

The log provides a slight caveat: the SQL aggregate failed_count did not match the campaign’s fixed accounts. The zero-failure rate is therefore proven by the k6 and /admin/storage checks, not by this unavailable aggregate. The 429 errors observed under load stem from the IP-based limiter and necessitate ensuring compliance with Retry-After.

What the switch means for OOBLIK

Photos, previews, PDFs and production artefacts now have their primary residence in France with a European provider, whilst the application and database are operated in Germany. This France-Germany split gives OOBLIK a clear EU framework for its customers’ data.

R2 remains accessible for read-only access during the grace period: sovereignty is not used as a pretext for removing the safety net too soon. A complete exit from Cloudflare, a second cross-provider copy and the final purge remain separate decisions to be taken at a later date.

title.text: Day 134 – The OVH switchover becomes proof of production

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Software used: Codex
  • Primary environment: Mac, KEREDIT dépôt local krampouz, GOF dépôt local gof, Hetzner Germany VPS and OVH 3-AZ Paris
  • Date covered: Monday 24 August 2026
  • Main branches: chore/k6-storage-provider-metrics, codex/portable-workflows and GOF branches of PRs #92/#93
  • Time window selected for the minimum: 10:56 – 19:30 CEST, cross-checked KEREDIT and GOF tracks
  • Minimum duration observed: approximately 8h34+
  • Release status: KEREDIT PRs #455/#456/#475 and GOF PRs #92/#93 merged into dev; 0.22.9 release deployed to production on the same day
  • Main changes: metric provider, k6 fixes, OVH key rotation, orphaned objects incident resolved and logged, 203/EXEC timer fix, portable workflows and purge of test data
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 874h47+ (866h13+ as at 23 August, +8h34+ today)

Quick read

The switchover is complete; the day is spent ensuring the evidence is preserved for the long term. The load reports finally distinguish the PUT time at the provider’s end, the Google Photos retries are consistent, and the log clearly documents what has been measured and what has not. At the same time, the rotation of OVH keys reveals the ACL model of the buckets, leading to the removal of the former POC user — and this deletion triggers a real incident: the objects become orphaned and unreadable for a few hours, before a step-by-step repair is carried out.

Client data sovereignty therefore does not depend solely on two countries on a map. It depends on the ability to explain where the data resides, who can access it, how the service is measured and how to roll back changes.

Don’t let a green benchmark become a legend

The k6 scripts isolate storage_put_duration, adhere to Retry-After and report n/a when a provider metric does not exist. The Google Photos scenario makes four consistent attempts and returns the last useful response. The report also specifies that the failed_count metric was not available during the 23 August campaign.

This honesty counts: OVH is significantly faster than R2 in the measurements carried out, but only the observations actually collected are attributed to the switch. The benefit of being based in France does not need a embellished figure to be significant.

The key points remind us that location alone is not enough

During the rotation, a new OVH S3 user receives ‘403 AccessDenied’ errors even though their keys are valid. The bucket belongs to the user who created it, and this service does not provide the expected bucket policies: the new user must be added to the ACL without revoking the owner’s grant.

The procedure is applied to krampouz-assets-prod, then the former POC user is revoked once the new keys have been propagated to KEREDIT and GOF. The runbook retains this specific provision for subsequent rotations. The storage is located in France; access to it must remain explicitly governed.

Deleting a user leaves their objects orphaned

The rest of the rotation proves that caution was justified, albeit painfully. The former POC user is deleted from the console by late morning, once the new keys have been verified. A few hours later, not a single thumbnail or image is displayed in the editor: each S3 object belongs to the user who created it, and deleting that user renders its 22,000 objects unreadable (403 AccessDenied on GET/HEAD, although the listing still works). The ACL for the successor’s bucket FULL_CONTROL does not change this, and PutObjectAcl is denied to non-owners.

The fix involves the R2 source, which has been kept as a fallback: a complete recursive copy of mc cp --recursive (rather than mc mirror --overwrite, which skips identical objects) to rewrite the 78 GB and transfer ownership to the new user. Variant generation jobs that fail during the maintenance window must be restarted via an explicit retry call, as BullMQ deduplication on jobId ignores simple re-adds. The publisher returned to normal operation that same evening, and the corrupted test data (12,295 assets, 3,016 projects, 13,112 orphaned objects) was purged correctly.

Two rules were added to the runbook to ensure no customer experiences this: never delete an S3 user before reassigning ownership of their objects, and never purge the source of truth before verifying readability by the successor. The R2 fallback, intended merely as a safety net, was used the very next day after the switchover.

KEREDIT and GOF maintain a common approach

The workflows for development, review, implementation and deployment are made portable between repositories. GOF now checks the origin of a release more strictly, and its CI no longer builds a runtime image for a purely documentary merge whilst monitoring the Docker context rules.

A patch also restores the executable bit on acceptance test scripts following a systemd failure (203/EXEC). This operational detail ties in with the main thread: a European infrastructure is only of value if the checks that validate it can actually be executed.

Status at the end of this post

KEREDIT and GOF use OVH 3-AZ Paris for production storage, with the application VPS in Germany and R2 still available for rollback during the grace period. The ‘0.22.9’ release is live, the campaigns are running smoothly, the measurement thresholds are documented, the orphaned objects incident has been resolved and its rules have been recorded in the runbook. What remains is long-term monitoring, a second copy with another European provider and, only at a later stage, the irrevocable decision to decommission R2.

title.text: Day 135 – Measuring sovereignty, closing blind spots

body.text:
Session timetable

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin on the left, code in the centre, Codex terminal on the right, GitHub Actions for PR validations
  • Date covered: Tuesday 25 August 2026
  • Main branches: codex/issue-458-save-concurrency, codex/issue-458-test-discovery, codex/release-0.23.1 and codex/issue-458-discovered-test-fixtures, all merged into dev
  • Window selected for the minimum: 00:10 – 09:59 CEST, from the first production lock to the merge of the final test isolation
  • Minimum observed duration: approximately 9 hours 48 minutes+
  • Version prepared: KEREDIT 0.23.1 and WordPress plugin 0.1.100; no evidence of runtime deployment observed today
  • Main traces: PR #485, #477, #490 and #491; stale backups, checkout/assets concurrency, web PDF permissions, exhaustive test discovery and isolation of the Google Photos queue
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 884h35+ (874h47+ as at 24 August, + 9h48+ today)

Quick read

The day begins ten minutes past midnight and feels less like a release than a long process of closing things down. The discovery of previously overlooked tests reveals a real-world issue: a client backup can still overwrite a field modified by an internal writer when that writer has not incremented the project version. Fixing this issue triggers a much broader review of concurrent writes relating to projects, assets, the WooCommerce checkout and web PDF permissions.

By the morning, four PRs have been merged. KEREDIT 0.23.1 is ready, but the log does not show it as deployed: the latest VPS version explicitly listed in the documentation remains 0.22.9. Today’s result is, firstly, a persistence contract that is harder to bypass, and secondly, a suite of tests that finally recognises all the files it needs to run.

A single version is not enough when several writers share the project

The first safeguard prohibits modifying a project whilst it is in active production . The core fix goes further: a versioned backup locks the project line, re-reads the fields it is about to write whilst under this lock, and returns ‘409 project_version_conflict’ if any of them have changed since the client snapshot. An internal update without a version bump can therefore no longer be silently overwritten by a save that has become stale.

The same requirement then extends to the other write paths. Asset mutations and the final checkout are fenced; the order of the deduplication locks is standardised; and storage deletions gain persistent intentions. Variants whose processing was interrupted can be resumed without losing their clean-up, and quotas are no longer adjusted based on a state that has become obsolete during the transaction.

This is a substantial undertaking because a process never operates in isolation. An administrative task, an import, a deletion or a job queue may all affect the same project with legitimate intent. The useful approach is not to assume a single writer; it is to make their order visible and to refuse the write when the freshness proof is no longer valid.

The checkout and web PDF are designed to fail safely

The WooCommerce workflow is hardened around the attempt ID, the ordered version and the expected payload. A divergent payload is rejected; a submitted order can be retrieved by its attempt ID; and an active reservation remains exclusive. Reconciliations are time-limited so that an old scan cannot arbitrarily link to a recent order.

Access to the web PDF follows the same logic. Authorisation for sharing becomes atomic; a disabled option is rejected and the deferred policy is locked before execution. When a repair fails and is then resumed, its dispatch line and commercial rights remain linked to the correct version of the project. The PDF is no longer merely an artefact to be produced: it remains the consequence of an explicit right, verified at the moment the system acts.

Tests now find files they previously overlooked

PR #477 replaces fragile globs with a recursive and portable detection method. The evidence attached to the PR counts 126 out of 126 backend files and 84 out of 84 frontend files, including two suites—photo_print—which were not being executed. The command `test:list` makes this inventory visible and any new file `*.test.ts` is automatically included in the contract.

This comprehensive check then reveals a residual dependency on the Redis queue shared in a Google Photos scenario. PR #491 replaces the actual BullMQ write with a local stub that checks the name, payload and jobId, then restores the original descriptor. The CI runs for all four PRs complete successfully; the comprehensive suite does not pass by masking the test that has just caused a problem.

Preparing 0.23.1 without reinventing the production process

The four application manifests pass at 0.23.1, the preparation documentation is aligned and the plugin remains ready at 0.1.100. Typecheck, lint, build, OKF validations and CI are reported as green in the relevant PRs.

However, no evidence has been found to confirm a VPS deployment of 0.23.1 today. This post maintains this distinction: the code has been merged and the release is prepared; the ‘live’ status should only be confirmed after checking the SHA and the version served by production.

Status at the end of the ticket

KEREDIT emerges from the night with a more explicit concurrency model, a checkout that rejects ambiguities, PDF permissions more firmly tied to their versions, and comprehensive test coverage. The number of fixes also highlights the cost of a review carried out right up to the transactional boundaries. The next useful step is not to add a new product promise: it is to keep this evidence accessible and to verify separately the release of the prepared version.

body.text:
Session timetables

  • Tool used: Codex
  • Main environment: VS Code WSL, Codex plugin on the left, code in the centre, Codex terminal on the right
  • Date covered: Wednesday 26 August 2026
  • Branch observed: dev, three documentation and clean-up commits

  • Minimum time observed: approximately 0h45+
  • Release status: no new releases or runtime deployments observed
  • Main traces: 4c31d50a, 9c8e4eba and 830fa929; removal of .claude, copies of .github/skills, references to slash commands and CLAUDE.md
  • Minimum cumulative time since the start of the log: approximately 885h20+ (884h35+ as at 25 August, + 0h45+ today)

Quick read

The session lasts less than an hour and removes over a hundred thousand lines. This contrast does not indicate a rewrite of the product: it indicates the removal of duplicate tools and instructions that have become obsolete. The slash commands from Claude Code are no longer in use; several snapshots of the impeccable skill duplicate source code managed elsewhere; and CLAUDE.md describes a CI as well as structural files that no longer correspond to the repository.

The clean-up brings an era to a close without denying its achievements. Before removing the last file, two rules that still hold true are saved in frontend/AGENTS.md: first, fill in the empty photo blocks and keep all the snapping logic within its canonical module.

Remove duplicates that create false context

The directories .claude/commands, .claude/skills and the copies at .github/skills are removed. They contained slash commands and bulky snapshots of skills that were no longer the current sources. Personal workflows now reside in locations managed by agents, whilst repository-specific instructions remain at .agents/skills and in the AGENTS.md files.

This removal reduces a real risk: an agent might have read an outdated copy, followed a command that no longer exists, or believed that a duplicate script was still being maintained. The number of lines removed is staggering, but the decision remains straightforward: a single, up-to-date source is better than several executable archives that are all similar.

CLAUDE.md should no longer compete with AGENTS.md

The latest commit removes CLAUDE.md. The file repeated part of the root instructions, including a CI statement that is now incorrect and an out-of-date list of important files. README.md, docs/HOME.md and the onboarding guide will therefore no longer refer to it as a starting point.

The workstation recovery procedure has been rewritten to start from AGENTS.md, docs/HOME.md, docs/KEREDIT/START_HERE_CODEX.md and the command guide. The change does not merely involve replacing one agent’s name with another: it restores the current documentation hierarchy as the focus of the next session.

Two rules remain because they still protect the product

The first rule retained stipulates that an image insertion must first fill an empty block, or create a new block, without silently replacing a photo that is already in place. The second rule sets frontend/src/lib/snapping.ts as the sole source of magnetic alignment and reminds the user to call setCoords() after a change of position during object:moving.

These two sentences would have been lost with CLAUDE.md if the clean-up had been purely mechanical. Their migration illustrates the correct approach: remove the obsolete container, re-read its contents, then transfer each invariant that is still valid to the instruction file of the domain that applies it.

Status at the end of this post

The product remains unchanged and no runtime publications are claimed. KEREDIT ends the day with less concurrent context, a role realignment in line with WSL and Codex, and two frontend invariants placed in the correct location. The Claude Code era remains visible in the log history; it no longer features as a second technical authority in the current repository.
